author: @fajarsetiawan8665
text:
​@acupppatea self-awareness is indeed a positive action. It is also hypocritical to deny that small changes from ourselves matter. However, things like this can be fishy when it comes to the so-called "awareness movement". In the movement, you'll see a process of ideologization which means putting your belief, and only yours, to a pedestal of perspective, making yourself believe that your sole idea is the truth and thus, other people should follow as well. What comes next is an agenda to widespread the belief through social engineering programs like campaigns, march, courses, etc.

The thing is, dissonance is real. Dissonance came when you are troubled on facing an inner conflict to your belief which often caused by a hot-headed confrontation or patronizing attitude. Like a delinquent who will climb a tree when you told him not to, we tend to act like that as well. 
Notwithstanding that at its extreme, movement can be anti-critic and politically opportunistic as they would use any means to defend their belief even if it does not necessarily ethical. This thing does not only happen in far-right and bigoted groups, but also in so-called progressive movement like MeToo, Pride, BLM, Green movement, etc.

What we must do is to change our approach to engage. An organic, digestible, and empathetical conversation, which is ironically very relatable to traditional social culture, can mend this hot-headed dissonance. Remember Nietzchean morality in which compassion, down-to-earth, and most importantly, reflective attitudes have a more powerful assertive effect than a direct intervention. Telling people to "step on other's shoes" is more compelling than "throwing a straight palm to their face". This way will be much more effective if you want to "discipline the customers".

- buy clothing made of natural fabrics
- buy less, but higher quality 
- swap clothes with friends 
- buy vintage
- buy handmade
- support local brands and local seamstresses 
- fix clothes

text:
I’m truly humbled by the overwhelming response to this video—thank you all for watching, sharing, and caring deeply about these issues. I wanted to address some of the most common comments:

Again, thank you for engaging with this discussion so thoughtfully. Your comments have given me a lot to reflect on!🙂

author: @StrayChoom
text:
It’s not a “consumerism” problem, it’s a capitalism problem. But cutting consumption does help a worker out. You can vote against it with your wallet, but you’ll lose the vote.

This is just the necessary result of capitalist imperialism. This exploitation and bad treatment is what private ownership of capital leads to in itself. And it doesn’t just apply to fast fashion, it applies to all companies. 

What this does not bring up is that these conditions for fast fashion are even worse in Bangladesh, who regularly employ child labour and pay even less. There are workers in the west and in the US who are paid less by the hour. This is not exclusive to China, or the fast fashion industry.

This stuff in the beginning of English capitalism was very common. We used child labour, so much so. And the capitalists fought tooth and nail to keep children, little boys and girls working themselves to death.

The thing is, none of it ever stopped. Once we outlawed it, well we still wanted cheap clothes that could only feasibly be made at that exchange value (price) via extremely exploitative means. So we then just buy the products of child labour from other countries, we even destabilise other countries and occupy their markets such that these products can be kept at such a cheap price. Which reproduces and normalises the exploitative practice.

I never buy from fast fashion, but what I have to say is not buying is not enough. You need to fight against capitalism - private ownership of capital by individuals.

It could be done away with as simply as slave owning (private ownership of labour) was done away with.

author: @ceekay3143
text:
I bet those working per piece are also not being compensated if their working conditions or employer decisions affect their ability to efficiently complete their work to the company standard. I mean, I was lucky to be on an hourly wage rather than per piece when I worked in a food factory, because the downtime was ridiculous. 


Lack of regular maintenance on machines leading to higher rates of product failure (product getting damaged/unusable), as well as equipment failure. Leading to having to hand package product at maybe 10 pieces per minute tops, compared to the machine at 50-100 per minute. This could last for a few minutes, to a few days, because of course we'd have to fly in a highly skilled expert to repair things when they got beyond what we could fix with a toolbox. And of course, loss from destroyed/wasted product and packaging materials during failures.
Like, I don't think Shein companies would be performing regular maintenance and servicing, or compensating workers for the pieces they would have been able to make if everything was in working order.


One of the worst weeks was when a whole shipment of (refrigerated) product was rejected due to temperatures being too high. Some asshat delivery driver decided to turn off refrigeration in the truck to save money on petrol, so at least the company had insurance and someone to compensate for the trouble. But we then us employees got to spend several hours going through the rejected/dead stock and separating food product from recyclable packaging, to reduce garbage costs. And no new product could be made and packaged while we were handling this and trying to clear out fridge space. 
Do Shein workers still get paid their cents per piece if that piece reaches the end of the production line and is rejected for quality issues before it leaves the warehouse? What if something happens on the way through to customers, and their order is refunded? I assume that Shein would be the one missing out on the money, buying the pieces from the garment companies, but I wouldn't put it past someone to punish the workers for this.

This is active, calculated ambition, not passive slavery.

they are fighting for survival.

text:
According to the man being interviewed in the video, 
All the range wages should actually be regarded as the minimum. 

For example,7000 CNY - 8500 CNY should be considered as 7000 CNY.
Based on that, the minimum wage shown in the video is 5500 CNY.
Those job with a salary of 5500 CNY involves job contents such as cutting wires, packaging, miscellaneous work, and flattening semi-finished products(Jobs that require almost no professional skills).
And The median salary in China is 4,485 CNY.

So, what do you mean by "low salary"?

According to the exchange rate 5500 CNY≈763 USD
According to the Purchasing Power Parity in different criteria 5500 CNY≈1617 USD-2750 USD

So, again, what do you mean by "low salary"?

Although every child in the office desires everyone to live by drink coffee and use the computers, But  the vast majority of the products you uses are not produced by drinking coffee and using computers.

So, what does a harsh working environment refer to? 
Does it refer to the scattered products and materials which lying on the ground?

According to the interview, the working hours for piece-rate jobs depend on the target salary.
If the project deadline is approaching, the factory will require overtime work or complete more products as soon as possible. 
However, the salary remains independent of the time and is only related to the production quantity.

So, You mean that a group of people，who earn more money than the median wage through long periods of physical labor ，produce goods that are affordable to those with lower wages than median wage, Is it a bad thing?

I don't know.

I hope that all the products that claim to be sturdy, well-made, high quality and fashionable can be sold in a price that people with wages below the median can afford to purchase.

Rather than promoting expensive, low quality and luxuriou fashion through ideological method.

I hope everyone can earn more by work harder, 
and the prices all around the world can keep dropping. 
Love and Peace.

I am Korean and travel to China twice a year, mainly to attend the Canton Fair. Watching this video has given me a lot to think about.

In Korea, many job seekers can rather easily earn around 17,000–20,000 RMB per month. They usually work only five days a week, and even then, their working hours rarely exceed 10 to 12 hours a day.

Delivery workers in Korea earn about 35,000–40,000 RMB per month, typically working six days a week for 10 to 12 hours each day.

Since I started importing products from China, I’ve become very interested in both the country and its people. I am also quite familiar with Shein as a company.

Given the demographic structure, I’m not sure how quickly these issues can be resolved. But seeing how many Chinese people struggle in their daily lives has given me a lot to reflect on.

Thank you for this meaningful video.

author: @bmk8018
text: It's easy for Westerners, from a position of privilege, to view the situation with disgust and judgment. And sure, that's understandable. no one would want to be in such conditions. However, reducing China's economic boom to just cheap labor and poor working conditions oversimplifies the issue and disregards the progress China has made in those areas. Every developed country has gone through similar phases at some point, and it’s not fair to impose our privileged standards on China without considering the potential unintended consequences, which could end up being worse than the current situation. It's easy to virtue signal when your GDP per capita is four to five times higher than the country you’re critiquing. While China is the second-largest economy by total GDP, it still lags far behind on a per capita basis compared to modern industrialized Western nations. Once countries reach a certain level of wealth, they can improve their standards of living, but imagine if we only had a fifth of our current income or GDP. our quality of life would be drastically reduced. So, this isn’t about justifying these conditions but about trying to understand them without oversimplifying or creating a caricature of an entire industry based on the perspective of one company. Drawing hasty conclusions or policies could lead to even worse outcomes for those affected.

author: @Wells-k5j
text:
I am a textile industry professional who has worked at Shein for five years.
China's textile and garment industry faces widespread and systemic issues: low wages, poor treatment, inadequate welfare systems, and widespread non-compliance with labor laws. Workers face high costs and barriers in defending their rights, making it difficult to sue employers. As a result, the government largely turns a blind eye to these practices.

It's not just Shein—suppliers for brands like JCPenney, Nike, GAP, and Old Navy also engage in similar tactics: cutting workers’ benefits in order to maintain profit margins.

Workers often don't get weekends off or receive overtime pay. They routinely work 12 hours or more per day. If they are injured on the job, compensation is minimal.

However, when American clients visit the factories for inspections, the factories often falsify records—hiding evidence of weekend overtime and instructing workers to lie. If a worker accidentally reveals the truth during an inspection, they are likely to be fined or even fired. These are desperate measures taken by factory owners simply to maintain—not increase—their profits, because the Chinese textile industry is under significant pressure.

Although Chinese labor is cheap compared to developed countries, it is still costly relative to Southeast Asia or Central America. To secure orders, Chinese factories are forced to continuously cut costs. The textile industry is not considered a high-priority sector by the government, so it receives little policy support. Workers’ welfare is neglected, and factories are pushed out of urban areas under the banner of "industrial optimization," relegated to regions with poorer conditions.

At a deeper level, I believe the root cause lies in the government's failure to assess whether labor resources and industrial structures in coastal cities are truly compatible. Industrial relocation policies have been implemented blindly, without considering the fate of low-income workers. As a result, these workers have no choice but to sacrifice their own well-being in exchange for a chance to survive in the city.

text:
The world is not fair, you know. Countries like Saudi Arabia can live like millionaires just by digging up oil, while the United States can simply print money and buy things from all over the world. The situation for Chinese workers is tough, yet it’s still better than in most other developing countries. That’s because China produces its own affordable industrial goods instead of relying on imports. In contrast, other developing nations have to import such goods from China, which makes the cost of living much higher.

Just want to start this conversation by stating that I'm poor, and disabled.  I already live well below the poverty line.  So what I'm saying is not coming from a place of 'privilege'.  I'm also a lifelong activist in more than one country.  But we need to stop making, and buying cheap things.  I don't buy things because they are cheap. We can say all we like about providing jobs etc, but these jobs frankly, never should exist.  Ditto to 'fast fashion'.  We need to supply sustainable ways of doing things, and then provide those jobs, AND compensate people properly.  

With the current state of the world, and what we know about something like plastic pollution alone, these things should not be allowed.  Full stop.  Thinking that we 'need' them, because 'what will poor people buy?' is the very classism that they think they are trying to avoid.  So, poor people should not have safe, quality things?  But dangerous, cheap things?  Just because they are poor?  This was not the case historically.  If you don't believe me, you can research it.  Poor people appreciated quality, and had nice things.  They made things last.  It's only a western, modern idea that we need to provide tons of cheap, toxic, low quality things for consumers to buy in surplus, and then throw away.  Never use to be a thing.  People valued what they had, and it wasn't necessarily cheap.  We need to rethink how we do everything, and raise the bar.  I never buy from these companies.  I need to know that what I'm supporting, is something good, and I also need to know that the product I am using does not have any harmful ingredients etc.

author: @genniebay6845
text:
just to put things into perspective—if you're being paid $0.05 per piece and earned $1,227 in a month, that means you had to produce about 24,540 pieces that month. Assuming you worked 20 days, that’s roughly 1,227 pieces per day.

If you worked 12 hours a day (including an hour for meals), that breaks down to about 111 pieces per hour, or nearly 1.8 pieces per minute—essentially one piece every 33 seconds, non-stop.

It’s hard to overstate how intense and relentless that is. Imagine doing this every single day, for months or even years, with little to no time or energy left to pursue anything else or improve your situation. If that’s not a tough reality, I honestly don’t know what is.

author: @Therese.Backman
text:
The commercial in the background with models on billboards is giving me hunger-games vibes. 

As a worker in Sweden I wake up at 06 with my kids, taking them to school, then I have a breakfast break for 30 min - 1 hour before starting work. I finish between 18 and 20.30 and it takes half an hour to get home (before I moved it took 1 hour with bus).
Some days I am off work completely and then I pick up my kids from school around 1 pm. During those days I clean the house, do grocery shopping and wash clothes.
I work in retail & they dont give us fulltime jobs.
 I work every second weekend aswell, home between 17-19.
I get paid so I can pay my rent, the bills and buy food. i only buy clothes second hand and sometimes fast fashion (like hm). I buy skincare frequently and makeup occasionally. I buy gifts for my kids on their birthdays and on Christmas. I get by and I think my life is very good compared to others but I don't love in luxury and I don't have any money in my bank account. To buy gifts to my children at Christmas I save 6 months in advance. I never go on holidays with my kids and travel abroad. I am a single mother of 2 without any drivers licence (cause I could never afford it) and my rent is 1350 $/month. I rent an appartement and I have to share bedroom with one of my kids because I can't afford a bigger flat. Food costs around 800-1000$/month because the prices kept going up but not our sallarys so much. I think my life is good, but it's not luxury and I live in Sweden in Europe

author: @punxsutawneyphilofficial
text:
I previously worked for a small, family run upholstery factory in the US. The conditions there weren't far off from this. We were more organized with less pieces on the floor or overflowing, but we still had unreasonable quotas, low wages, and a massive wealth disparity between the owners and workers. 3 brothers owned it and at least one of the brothers owns a ~620K house. Most of my coworkers were renting or living with family (including myself). The owners of the factory would pull up in BMWs while the workers had beat up Nissans. 

It was for a company with MUCH higher profit margins too. The brand would sell office chairs for about $1K a pop. There'd be dayS where I sewed hundreds of office chair seats and brought home maybe $700/week before taxes. I totaled an order I was making once of 94 chairs and they would have been about $120K. I made $140 that day (before taxes). We also had to do mandatory overtime of an extra 5-10hrs/week. The money was nice but it takes an extreme toll on your body. 

Health hazard wise, we had an entire wall covered with black mold that the owners said they'd take care of, I got carpal tunnel from repetitive sewing but had to continue working through it, and one of my coworkers once sewed over her finger and the needle got stuck. She pulled it out with some pliers and kept going. We may get paid more, but working conditions in American factories aren't sunshine and rainbows either.

author: @TheJoyNinjaNZ
text:
I've worked inside garment factories in New Zealand just like this - cramped, piles of garments everywhere, hot, loud.  I have worked for a piece rate, where you have to be very accurate and very very fast to make any kind of living.  It is the nature of garment production and it was no different in Victorian times.  What has evolved in the 'Western world" is labour protection laws, human rights laws, child protections, etc at the same time as *rampant consumerism*  We know we can't treat workers like this our shores, but we're more than willing to turn a blind eye to other countries' labour practices to get a steady supply of cheap goods.  

The real shame is the skill and craftmanship that goes into garment production takes years to hone - it doesn't matter what country you're in you should be paid fairly!  I think its tragic that Shein's business model obscures the skill and potential a very well trained Chinese labour force has to bring beautifully made, quality items to the world.  The fact is - NZ used to have that skilled labour force but they let the industry die.

author: @ixeliema
text:
God. This is very much my "I knew it was bad but jfc" moment. I bought some swimwear and shirts via Shein back in 2019 after first hearing about them from a college friend, since I'd mentioned many of my clothes and shoes being over 7 years old and beginning to show their age. They'd sold me on the idea with their low prices, and being naïve I really didn't consider why that might have been, namely because I needed to save as much money as possible given my roommate just bailed and left me and my partner paying a rent we couldn't afford. I bought some stuff, and literally found out they were somewhat known for their practices being bad like, a week later. 

Part of me felt like "well if it's just fast fashion bad I can just make this shit last, that's exactly the opposite of what the industry pledges to be," but I had a feeling it was worse, given I found somewhat recent art theft accusations as well. I had considered returning the items, if for no other reason than personal moral absolvment, but I didn't have the energy to go through the hassle of that as a full-time student, so I kept it all. I still have all those things now, but almost entirely bc I barely wear them compared to sturdier, less shrunken, clothing I own (my favorite pair of yoga pants is 15 years old and only just now has holes). Seeing Shein get more and more exposure as a severely shitty company company over the last half a decade, I almost wish I had gone to the trouble of returning it back then, just to cause a bit of annoyance to the higher ups of Shein, but the fact is that a company that huge would never have made it their problem to deal with any consequences...plus 50 bucks is a drop in the bucket for a company like that. I just know some poor underpaid overworked person working some ungodly shift hours would've gotten stuck cleaning up the situation. I still look at those items with a sick feeling in my gut, and I still live paycheck to paycheck. Sometimes it's tempting to try to fill out my waning wardrobe with something new, especially as I am quite low on professional attire atm, but I always remember that whatever money I have and whatever life I am complaining about, I am still nowhere near the level of suffering that the people in Shein's grasp are. And that makes me so angry. But what else can I do? I wish there was anything else I could feasibly do. I sincerely appreciate the people who go to bat for those suffering 8-10s, I share those stories (as many comments have said, this is very much some incredible journalism on your part). I just avoid and encourage avoidance. But that's never going to feel like enough. I wish the average American had any more ability to help. This is just utterly miserable. What a fucking nightmare.

author: @patient-investor
text:
Thank you for this thoughtful and the behind-the-scenes look into the factories producing for Shein. Exposing these working conditions is crucial for holding brands accountable and sparking informed public debate. One point often overlooked in these conversations is the structure of Shein’s supply chain: the company doesn’t own its factories but contracts work to third-party operators. These factory owners, often local entrepreneurs can benefit from such contracts, creating a ladder of upward mobility in regions where economic opportunities are limited. While the system is far from perfect, it can offer a route out of poverty not only for workers, but also for small-scale entrepreneurs.

At the same time, we shouldn’t excuse the exploitative aspects of this model. Reports of excessive working hours, withheld wages, and unsafe conditions are deeply troubling and deserve serious scrutiny. But we also need to place this within the broader context of global manufacturing and labor. In many cases, workers in Shein-affiliated factories earn more than entry-level office workers in Chinese tier-one cities such as Shanghai, raising questions about how we define “exploitation” across different socio-economic landscapes. If our concern is truly worker dignity and fair labor, we must resist reducing this to a single villain narrative and instead confront the systemic drivers: fast fashion’s demand for speed and volume at low cost, and our collective complicity as consumers.

This broader lens brings companies like Amazon into the conversation, despite being based in highly developed nations with strict labor laws, yet still consistently criticized for abusive warehouse practices. Unlike Shein, Amazon directly employs its warehouse staff, which means it holds full accountability for working conditions. And yet, reports persist of workers being injured at high rates, facing relentless productivity quotas, and being penalized for basic human needs like bathroom breaks. In this case, there is no intermediary to absorb the blame. The exploitation is institutional and happening within legal systems that should offer greater protection. 

Food for thought to engage in dialogue

text:
I'm surprised by how high the pay is! Considering China's low cost of living, I was expecting Shein to be paying less than 3,000 CNY per month for these workers. I'm more surprised by how little Shein pays per piece. Only pennies per piece per worker? Changing it from, say 5 to 10... would double worker compensation, but only be a minor increase to the company as a whole. Considering apartments near the Shein Village start around 3,000 CNY, and workers already earn double to triple that depending on overtime... It's a shame the workers don't benefit more from the low margin business model.

Here in the US, low skill manufacturing pays at or near minimum wage, and a beginner apartment in US might be as low as 7,000 CNY if you're in one of the few lowest cost cities, but more likely 10,000 to 20,000 CNY per month for an apartment with 1 or less bedrooms.  Typical monthly wage in US for that kind of work is 12,000 - 22,000 CNY depending on local wages. Barely enough for beginner housing! Is the Chinese worker still better off compared to one in the US?

author: @GreenPartyofMalaysia
text:
Shein, a leading force in the global fast-fashion industry, continues to face significant criticism over labour rights violations within its supply chain. Despite public pledges to uphold ethical sourcing and employment standards, recent audits and investigations have uncovered ongoing issues including child labour, excessive working hours, and insufficient wages.

Child Labour Cases

In 2024, Shein disclosed the discovery of two instances of child labour within its supplier network—matching the number identified in 2023. The minors involved were reportedly aged 11 years and eight months, and 15 years and three months, respectively. Upon discovery, Shein severed ties with the offending suppliers and reiterated its commitment to preventing such breaches. That year, the company claimed to have carried out approximately 4,300 audits covering 317,000 workers, as part of its efforts to increase scrutiny over labour practices.[^1]

Excessive Hours and Substandard Pay

Investigative reporting and labour rights organisations have repeatedly documented cases of workers in Shein’s supply chain being subjected to extreme work conditions. Employees at some supplier factories have been found working up to 75 hours per week, far exceeding legal limits. In many cases, these excessive hours are paired with wages well below living standards—raising concerns about the exploitation of vulnerable workers to sustain the brand’s ultra-fast fashion cycle.[^2]

Opaque Supply Chains and Enforcement Weaknesses

Shein’s business model—characterised by speed, volume, and a reliance on a sprawling network of third-party suppliers—makes oversight particularly challenging. While the company has instituted a Supplier Code of Conduct and conducts regular audits, experts and critics argue that these measures often fail to detect or prevent labour abuses in practice. Despite Shein’s recent attempts to boost transparency and engagement with external monitors, allegations persist that systemic issues remain unaddressed.[^3]

Consumer Responsibility and Industry Impact

The controversy surrounding Shein is symptomatic of wider ethical concerns in the fast-fashion sector. The pressure to produce cheap clothing at scale often leads to the erosion of workers’ rights. Growing awareness among consumers, however, is prompting calls for more transparent sourcing practices and for shoppers to make informed decisions that support fair treatment of labour.

In conclusion, although Shein has undertaken measures to improve accountability, the recurrence of serious violations underscores the need for ongoing vigilance and structural reform. Ethical concerns around the company’s supply chain remain unresolved, and it is likely that continued public and regulatory pressure will be necessary to enforce lasting improvements.

In many cases, these excessive hours are paired with wages well below living standards—raising concerns about the exploitation of vulnerable workers to sustain the brand’s ultra-fast fashion cycle.[^2] Opaque Supply Chains and Enforcement Weaknesses Shein’s business model—characterised by speed, volume, and a reliance on a sprawling network of third-party suppliers—makes oversight particularly challenging. While the company has instituted a Supplier Code of Conduct and conducts regular audits, experts and critics argue that these measures often fail to detect or prevent labour abuses in practice. Despite Shein’s recent attempts to boost transparency and engagement with external monitors, allegations persist that systemic issues remain unaddressed.[^3] Consumer Responsibility and Industry Impact The controversy surrounding Shein is symptomatic of wider ethical concerns in the fast-fashion sector. The pressure to produce cheap clothing at scale often leads to the erosion of workers’ rights. Growing awareness among consumers, however, is prompting calls for more transparent sourcing practices and for shoppers to make informed decisions that support fair treatment of labour. In conclusion, although Shein has undertaken measures to improve accountability, the recurrence of serious violations underscores the need for ongoing vigilance and structural reform. They'd wear the pieces around town for a season, then have their dressmaker rework them for common wear around the house or pass down to servants or poorer family members. Even rich women back then could usually fill just an average armoire and dresser, and that was that--whereas now average women own pounds and pounds of poorly made crap. Huge dumps of clothing to landfill was unheard of back then.

text:
Yeah I’ve worked 8am-12am shifts six days a week for a year and couldn’t afford to pay rent in the US.  We can’t all be choosy with where to buy clothes. That money isn’t going to the workers, it’s going to the ceo. Your option to avoid fast fashion is to go to specialist small businesses but they have rates so high people living paycheck to paycheck can’t just “save up” for that.

The problem is fundamentally capitalism, not the people suffering under it that are subject to its rule.

author: @hyui5096
text:
​@Elennar29 Im sorry but you are does feel like you are a bit ignorant when being virtuous about the whole subject. First off, many company like Shein is a chinese company or an company from the country of manufacture and then they sell to other countries. Less so for shoes but certainly for clothing.

Next off these big businesses are not "greedy". Sure some of them are but the idea of this generalisation is just inaccurate. For example, Shein operates with a razor thin profit margin of 2-8% meaning that these "greedy" companies are passing on all those low prices to "greedy" consumers. The fast fashion industry was not created by these big businesses. It was created by consumers when the old fashion system was outcompeted by consumers buying more cheap fast fashion items.

Next $1.5 in Vietnam is not bad compared to the average wage in Vietnam. You can have a google but it is 1.5-3x the average wage. And not buying from these companies just leaves cities of people jobless. Not give them better working conditions. The only reason they are working there is that they cannot find a better job. The thing is most of them have incredibly long hours with no breaks. The pay itself is not terrible.

Clothing/shoes have alot more costs then just labour. From tarriffs to middlemans to the material used to the cost of machinery maintaince ,  none of these "greedy big businesses" have high profit margins unless you are talking about designer stuff. They make money from quantity and the workers get little money because their labour isn't worth alot. The reason of that is complex from education to lack of transportation to lack or opportunities but it certain is not because they have more options.

If people want to help these workers then they should donate to charity the money that they saved from buying off Shein instead of transferring blame to another party to feel better and more ethical. The truth is, The world is tough and to alot of people, being angry at a faceless third party, is alot easier the acknowledging that no one is to blame and it is just this because consumers want to cheaper stuff from countries less developed.

text:
I agree that consumerism is a problem, but it's not the only one.

Normal and higher end brands also are participating in this, exploiting workers, paying small wages. 

Clothes that are made worldwide are not made to last long, so the consumers are forced to throw away and buy.

People buy things to cope with every day life, with their unhappiness, to get a little bursts of it, they are manipulated to buy more and more and to fall into addiction, some have undiagnosed mental issues and it can be even harder for them. Probably there are more reasons of consumerism, I'm not a specialist. But I know changing all of that shouldn't be put on the shoulders of common people, yes they should be aware and do what they can, but we need systemic change.

So we then just buy the products of child labour from other countries, we even destabilise other countries and occupy their markets such that these products can be kept at such a cheap price. Which reproduces and normalises the exploitative practice.

I never buy from fast fashion, but what I have to say is not buying is not enough. You need to fight against capitalism - private ownership of capital by individuals.

author: @Yilin-LynXYilin
text:
In cartoons from the 2000s (or even earlier), the main character always wore the same outfit for the whole season—and I love that. I’m not trying to debate whether fashion in animation is important (ofc it is), but I work in the animation industry, which is why I used animation as an example. When I said the main character only has one outfit, I didn’t mean we literally draw them only one set of clothes, but rather that they usually have one signature outfit that’s well designed for them. For example, Detective Conan, Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba, and Chainsaw Man. Fashion in animation is also closely tied to the production team’s budget.

Now, do you think someone like Zuckerberg or Jobs, who always wears the same style, is an NPC? I have a lot of clothes, but even if I were naked, I still wouldn’t consider myself an NPC. Wear as many clothes as you want, but don’t buy extra just because you’re afraid of being ignored or judged. Everyone is the main character in their own world, but in other people’s worlds, even if you have a thousand outfits, you may still just be a passerby. Being a main character isn’t determined by the number of clothes you own—it’s determined by the story you live.

author: @chrisabc123
text: I worked in sourcing based in Guangzhou 2002 to 2005 and then Hong Kong until 2020. Travelled China extensively. So much, that my Chinese colleagues would joke I know it better than them. It was amazing to see the industrial revolution unfold in front of my own eyes and how for example I would take a rickety bus from Hangzhou to Yuyao to visit a light factory in the beginning and near the end of my time there I was taking high speed rail. Generally labour practices that I witnessed were ok although rising labour cost was always the number one complaint of factory owners coupled with the constant pressure of lower prices from foreign buyers because the barriers to entry for competitors was so ridiculously low. I am not trying to explain way Shein. In fact I do what I can to persuade my peers to never buy the brand. That and anything on Temu which is just a covid era dumping ground for defective and unwanted production orders.  But from the economic side, I believe sadly we will only see the labour practices, compensation, etc improve in China with the help of the government. And I am afraid that given the sheer size of the manufacturing world in China, it truly could be an insurmountable task for the government. Great work Cinthia and thank you for allowing me to reminisce about a world I truly miss. Keep up the good work but please 小心.

author: @takotakotakotakotako
text:
Clothes are essential. Nobody is allowed to walk around without them, and they protect us from the weather as well. It should be unacceptable to treat the people who work on that business the way these are being treated. Sadly, this isn't just exclusive to fast-fashion business models like Shein or Alibaba. 

I personally know a person who has a fashion design degree, and the only job they got from it was working for small brands as a freelancer. Their work conditions are extremely similar to those. The only difference is that their workshop is at their parent's place, but they spend day and night sewing clothes for small brands, getting paid scraps by each piece sewn together, sometimes designing a piece themself, for brands that sell each garment for 10-15x the price they pay their workers to produce them. They can work in their pjs and from home, but they have no break days. No clear schedule. Only extreme micromanagement (to the point they had to get an extra phone line to avoid getting contacted by bosses on days/hours off), extra short deadlines, low monthly wage. Their body and mind suffer from it, but they don't know how to escape that life. Maybe it's been going on for so long that they learned to believe that it can't be helped, or that they don't deserve any better since they developed that skill out of their own volition. And I don't know if I can even help them in any way, given they stopped reaching out or responding to me.

@aesaphyr  "These companies make huge profits"

Lmao no they don't, wtf are you on about. The companies with the lowest wages are consistently the ones with the lowest profit margins, the companies with the highest profit margins, e.g tech, actually pay the highest wages.

This idea that companies can just get away with massive profits while they underpay workers is one of the wildest myths I see everywhere and it's so sad because people could just look at the profit margins of various companies and industries, it's publicly available information, the companies that struggle the most with worker wages are also, consistently, the ones with the lowest profit margins. This is true of Walmart, Shein, Temu, and pretty much every other retail company that competes on price, the whole idea is to sell a large volume at a razor thin margin.

The whole reason why companies are hiring people below minimum wage is because the minimum wage is too high, if the government cracks down on those companies, they won't raise their wages, they'll collapse and the workers will lose their jobs and they'll actually be worse off than you think they are now.

The actual solution to this kind of poverty is the long and tedious work of economic growth, when that happens more and more people get lifted out of poverty and wages rise, and working conditions improve. There are no shortcuts.

text:
@sinnella1 Blaming everyday consumers isn’t just unhelpful it’s unrealistic. Most people are just trying to survive, not run international supply chain investigations every time they buy a phone. If you actually care about labor exploitation, focus on pushing for real policy change—support international labor reform, pressure governments and corporations directly, or get involved in activism that targets the actual systems enabling abuse. The real solution lies in politics, labor rights, and international policy—not in performative consumer shaming. The world doesn’t revolve around the U.S., and everyday people shouldn’t be expected to carry the weight of fixing systemic exploitation.

text: @jj4774ns-te5px I'm relearning to sew (I sewed a little as a kid), and I try not to buy anything new when I can help it, so I get a lot of the fabric I use from this secondhand store in my city which sells damaged clothing by the pound at a low price. I don't take any of it regardless of color or pattern or how much there is to work with, because I can tell it would be a nightmare to try and sew without even trying. author: @regs3941
text:
Speaking for someone living in a Western industrial country: 
I never believed, that there are *so many* people out there, who can't afford somewhat sustainable alternatives to fast fashion. Clothing is by any means so cheap - yes, sustainable options included, if you don't go for brands and regular changes to your wardrobe. I say this as a person, who is poor herself by my country's poverty standard. 
The first sustainable alternative everybody got, is available to everyone: Do not by anything at all. 99% of us have more stuff, we even need.
Then comes repairing what you got. I do it all the time. Clothes - even cheap ones - can be worn so much longer then the average person keeps their fast fashion pieces. So, the low quality of fast fashion was never a valid argument for me to hear - most pieces aren't worn until the break down at all.
And the final cheap option for sustainable clothing: thrifting. You can get some high quality clothes for the price of SHEIN clothes. And not producing anything is *always* more sustainable then the ecologically friendliest production can be.

Oh, and sustainable new clothes do not cost much and are even cheaper if you calculate cost per wear. You just can't go after brands. I buy my leggins, that I wear under my skirts in winter from a sustainable company, who produces in Europe. The last thick winter leggings I bought was 22€ and it lasted me two winters and I wore it *often*. So, I can simply not say, that 44€ per winter is too much for me to pay and I can only afford the 10€ leggings from a fast fashion place (which would propably don't last that long, thus only last me half as long, so no money saved here).

author: @sk8razer
text:
6:56 "low budget" is an extremely important aspect. The discussion around fast fashion & sustainable fashion tends to center on people who can afford to over consume fast fashion. 

This video spends around 15 seconds total acknowledging that some people consume fast fashion for financial reasons. "Girl's got a point, not everyone can afford sustainable." at the absolute end of the video is the extent that the writers & producers decided to deviate from the overall message about financially comfortable people killing the planet via reckless over consumption. 

The message winds up being "You could and *SHOULD* invest the same amount of money in a decently sized, versatile wardrobe of sustainable items." with a whole list of tips like "keep your closet fresh by purchasing a few new items from sustainable designers each season to pair with items from last season!" 

It's great advice for that one specific demographic. But there's a lot of people relying on fast fashion's low price points just to keep themselves and their children clothed at all. 

Especially since another common tip is "Hit up thrift shops and second hand stores to get your fashion fix. Cute vintage pairs perfectly with socially & eco conscious, fashionista!". The increased demand from consumers who are able to spend more is doubly problematic for  people who lack as much expendable income. 

The supply obviously decreases, which increases the price point on its own. But price point is further increased by the fact that people with more expendable income are simply willing to pay more. 

There's a lot to say about the phenomenon of using thrifting as an altruistic way to over consume clothing ("I'm not just keeping *my* clothing out of a landfill in the global south, I'm literally keeping the clothing of other people out of landfills too! It's a win-win!"). But the key point here is that swapping fast fashion over consumption for over consumption of second hand items is not a win-win. 

There is no altruistic or guilt free swap for over consumption. Over consumption is *the* problem. 

Decreased access to used clothing forces lower income people to rely more on fast fashion options, including brick & mortar retailers like Walmart, Forever 21, and H&M. These lower quality new items are worn over and over for as long as possible. Fast fashion items are basically treated as "disposable" by fashion-focused higher income shoppers. But they don't actually become unwearable after a few wears (usually lol). 

The dyes start to fade and print starts to crack & peel very quickly. The fabric starts stretching  and thinning causing the garment to lose its original fit quickly. Wearable/repairable rips are fairly common. Basically, the item starts to look old and "frumpy" early on. But a lot of fast fashion options can be worn & washed multiple times per month for several months to a few years before finally becoming unwearable. 

But wear isn't the only driver behind necessary purchasing. Body shapes & sizes change, particularly if you're trying to keep children clothed. Items get lost or destroyed by forces beyond normal wear. The purchases made by people who rely on inexpensive options may be done in moderation and almost entirely out of necessity, but it adds up. 

More importantly, the percentage of people who rely on inexpensive items is much larger than the percentage of people who can afford more expensive sustainable items. We like to think that the fast fashion industry is entirely the result of shady marketing practices & "fashion industry culture" manipulating consumers in to rampant over indulgence. Like the people in these haul Tik Toks are wholly representative of fast fashion consumers. 

But a massive percentage of the market share lacks the ability to be manipulated into over indulgence. Because you can't be manipulated into buying more than you need if you can barely afford what you legitimately need. 

Fixing the over consumption problem among those in "comfortable" financial positions will only have a modest impact in the overall problem. To textile industry's widespread exploitation of workers and impact on the planet *feels* fairly isolated and easy to fix. "Just make better choices." is the common message. And those privileged people who have the ability to "just make better choices" absolutely should. 

Unfortunately, the problem is incredibly complex and completely enmeshed with the systems that make living so unaffordable for most of the planet's population. We can't do much to fix the social & ecological problems associated with fast fashion until we make significant progress on the sheer unavailability of being middle-income or lower. 

And we can't make any progress on that issue as long as we continue fixating on the personal responsibility aspect of individual finances. The problem goes far beyond simple financial irresponsibility and an unwillingness to "put in the work" to attain a more comfortable financial position. Financial illiteracy is only a small part of the situation. The actual problem is rigid hierarchies is profoundly broken systems.

The fabric starts stretching and thinning causing the garment to lose its original fit quickly. Wearable/repairable rips are fairly common. Basically, the item starts to look old and "frumpy" early on. But a lot of fast fashion options can be worn & washed multiple times per month for several months to a few years before finally becoming unwearable. But wear isn't the only driver behind necessary purchasing. Body shapes & sizes change, particularly if you're trying to keep children clothed. Items get lost or destroyed by forces beyond normal wear. The purchases made by people who rely on inexpensive options may be done in moderation and almost entirely out of necessity, but it adds up. More importantly, the percentage of people who rely on inexpensive items is much larger than the percentage of people who can afford more expensive sustainable items. We like to think that the fast fashion industry is entirely the result of shady marketing practices & "fashion industry culture" manipulating consumers in to rampant over indulgence. Like the people in these haul Tik Toks are wholly representative of fast fashion consumers. But a massive percentage of the market share lacks the ability to be manipulated into over indulgence. Because you can't be manipulated into buying more than you need if you can barely afford what you legitimately need. Fixing the over consumption problem among those in "comfortable" financial positions will only have a modest impact in the overall problem. To textile industry's widespread exploitation of workers and impact on the planet *feels* fairly isolated and easy to fix. "Just make better choices." is the common message. And those privileged people who have the ability to "just make better choices" absolutely should. Unfortunately, the problem is incredibly complex and completely enmeshed with the systems that make living so unaffordable for most of the planet's population. We can't do much to fix the social & ecological problems associated with fast fashion until we make significant progress on the sheer unavailability of being middle-income or lower. And we can't make any progress on that issue as long as we continue fixating on the personal responsibility aspect of individual finances. The problem goes far beyond simple financial irresponsibility and an unwillingness to "put in the work" to attain a more comfortable financial position. Financial illiteracy is only a small part of the situation. The actual problem is rigid hierarchies is profoundly broken systems.

author: @akiriwe
text:
I didn't ever buy anything in SHEIN, but after the war began, we were stuck in Germany with a little number of garments, and we used to make a couple of hauls to Primark to replenish the lack of cloth (we left Ukraine at the end of winter so we didn't have spring/summer cloth at all).

What can I say? Not proud of it. Didn't even worth it, really. One little example. Shoes might cost 10-20 euros, but they live only 2-3 months - I ruined 2 pairs of shoes over the 4 months, they were painful to wear, and I had blisters and damaged skin on my feet. You can argue it's justified, but look - I bought a pair of sneakers for 70 euros in October and I still wear them, they are in good condition and I am sure they will survive another couple of seasons easily. By this moment I would throw away 3-4 pairs of Primark shoes already, and, mind you, in terms of money you don't actually spend less. You buy low-quality, low-comfort shoes which will break apart soon enough and you will have to replace them. And the damage was quite significant, it's not like it got one small thing and I am throwing them away. Still, there are some good garments we took from there which are still alive and look good - jeans onesies, and some t-shirts are serving their purpose for a year already. But you have to know what to take.

After this experiment, I decided to go with rather rare shopping, but with better quality cloth from more responsible (or at least less reckless) brands, which will last longer and will look better One-two pairs of good jeans per year is enough. A couple of T-shirts, 1-2 pair of shoes. I am privileged enough now to afford myself to make a better choice, and I am lucky not to have fashion as an interest, but I know there are people as well, who will buy those 10 euros sneakers and will be forced to somehow walk in them for a long time, even if they become damaged, and I understand that and I have no judgment. My only concern is when people prefer to buy 10 pairs of 10 euro shoes just to have the ability to choose them depending on mood and throw them away a month later (I doubt those SHEIN bloggers didn't have money), not when the decision is made out of extreme poverty.

author: @Alexanderxu-k1x
text:
Why do consumers have to tolerate SHEIN - a unofficial Gulag?
As most Western consumers know, every successful or failed Chinese company is full of forced labor and various illegal activities, because in China, companies with deep ties to the government like Huawei and Shein can always regard the law as joke. However, even among these companies, Shein is probably the worst one.
There are two main points of shein's bad behavior

1. Ignore the labor law and force overtime through verbal communication from the manager when refusing to pay remuneration. From the beginning of 2023, in the face of competition from Pinduoduo, ByteDance and other similar products from other Chinese companies, shein began to force employees to work overtime without pay through managers at all levels, although most of the overtime hours did not yield any benefits. For example, according to confirmed information, Haiwei Yu, the senior manager of Shein's operations department, requires team members to work 40 hours of unpaid overtime per month. Yi Gao, the manager of the core trading department, requires team members to work at least 45 hours of unpaid overtime per month. In addition, it is said that Bie Shen, the manager of the commodity department, requires overtime to exceed 55 hours per month. Although overtime work is common in China, almost all other companies will pay full overtime pay, such as Huawei and Pinduoduo. Maybe some consumers feel that the market is free, and they can leave their jobs if they don’t want to, but the peculiarity of Shein is that it is good at using non-compete agreements. Go to the so-called competitors, but almost all similar companies in China are blacklisted by shein, which means that leaving shein is basically equivalent to never finding a job. Shein created a folk version of the "Gulag Islands" in this way. Everyone on the island has to work for a long time under low wages, not only office workers, but factories are no exception. There were once factory workers who couldn't bear it. Working long hours puts a distress note in the clothes that are sent to the US. Some Western consumers wonder why employees don’t sue the company and organize strikes to protest, because in China, facing companies like Shein, which can provide high taxes, the rulers have always condoned and severely cracked down on various worker protests.

2. Racial discrimination, the policy of recruiting employees in the United States distinguishes races. According to reliable sources, shein clearly gives priority to recruiting Chinese in the United States, especially those born and raised in China, because in the eyes of shein executives, these people have been subjected to dictatorship and oppression for a long time and are used to submitting, and employees of other races also prefer non-democratic countries These behaviors run counter to American values. Can Western consumers, especially American consumers, tolerate such behaviors that openly trample on the bottom line of society?


Most western consumers are definitely not interested in what happens in China, they only care about the cheap women's clothing provided by shein. However, even Western companies operating in China try their best to respect Zhou’s labor laws and maintain the humane traditions of Western society. For example, Suzhou Microsoft paid N+12 high compensation for layoffs. Shein is not the only one that can provide cheap products on this planet. Hope consumers can resist shein on the basis of universal values and promote it to change.

text:
I am guilty of buying clothes from Shein and other fast fashion, but I don't buy the trendy or cheap clothing items, I look for their 'normal priced' clothing items that fit my budget and has good reviews about the material and quality.  I'm a small person with body type that is not typical of where I live, often I found I can only find things that fit me from some of these fast fashion places. I also only look at Shein when I need clothes, and my clothes normally stay with me for years. They are not 'super high quality' , but they are nice and comfortable, and they have lasted. Only a couple of them actually end up break, ironically, the more 'fragile' ones were some of my more expensive items. However I mend them because I simply can't afford to throw them away. Even more ironically, I bought a few things from a local brand that market themselves as sustainable, locally made and environmentally conscious. Despite them being relatively more expensive, they end up being my least worn items and the fabrics are quite low in quality in comparison to the rest of my 'fast fashion' wardorbe. 

I do believe we can still buy from fast fashion places without overconsume. However I do really hate how these brands praying on young people with their ugly marketing strategies. But I think the root of the problem is that people simply don't know how to recognise good products and don't look after their clothes. Also, everything is so expensive these days.

text:
@susannpatton2893I definitely would, if I had that skill.  With my current skills, that would just be a fate worse than what's already available at Lane Bryant or Torrid. Lol

It's easy to say, "Just make it yourself", but I've never had to make my own clothes to find something that would fit me and be cute.  Also, it isn't fair to put that responsibility on only plus-sized people, who may have medical or genetic conditions.  

What about the people who make the fabric? What are their working conditions like? Are you going to make your own iPhone or laptop computer because some of the raw materials are mined by children in India?  Any person who is able to participate on YouTube has other people working for them in extremely unfortunate situations, they're just a few steps further back in the chain of production and are may be treated even worse than the people making clothes at SheIn.  Sadly, it's nearly impossible to live a harm free life. 

If we really want to tackle this issue of unfair working conditions, we have to fix our own problems. Why are people trying to get clothes that are so cheap? author: @rockingpinaple
text:
We can't push the responsibility to buy sustainable products onto consumers... Not just because it unfair or unrealistic (even though it is) but because it's not going to happen. It's wishful thinking. You'd need *everyone* to change their habits in order for this to make a difference. "Voting with your wallet", while cute, only serves to make you feel better because if only 10-15% votes for the environment (and I do believe I'm inflating those numbers right now), you loose this vote.

Vote with your... well, votes. The unfair competition could ONLY be evened out by legislation, for example introducing financial penalties for excessive environmental damage caused by the entity. It would encourage the companies to be more sustainable since leeching off of the environment would no longer be that profitable, it would make products that already are more competitive, and companies unwilling or unable to adapt would die a natural death. And there is a myriad other smart legal solutions that could be mixed and matched to help solve this problem.

author: @user-ll4cu5dh3b
text:
I roll my eyes when I see comments claiming you need to buy expensive designer brand clothing for it to be durable... 

Even fast fashion brands like Shien, Zara, and H&M have durable clothes if you just look for the clothing made with good material - although you may have to pay a slightly more premium than the $3 price tag. Stop feeling obligated to purchase luxury brands because that's simply marketing. The best recourse to this situation is: buying less clothing, becoming more knowledgeable about durable fabrics/materials so that the clothing you do purchase last at least for a few years, and finally thrifting or wearing second hand clothes. [An additional and helpful investment would be learning how to sew so that you can make repairs on softer damaged clothes, making them last even longer].

It's bizarre when people blame "fast fashion" (usually equating it to affordable clothing companies like H&M and Zara) for environmental problems when it's consumers purchasing an excessive amount of clothing that's the issue. I.e., if luxury goods were as cheap as SHEIN, it would create a nearly identical problem as SHEIN. The only reason why luxury brands are not included in this discussion (when they should be) is because there is a much higher cost of entry on how many and how much people are willing to spend for the products, which doesn't say much about how the companies, themselves, are tackling this issue. 

People should treat clothing like food: you're not going to know you're purchasing healthy food by looking at the brand or the price tag of the item, but you will know if you look at its nutritional label. Likewise, if you want durable or environmentally friendly clothing, look at the material of the clothes. Furthermore, you can't just eat an inordinate amount of healthy food to be healthy; you need to diet properly to be healthy. Therefore, if you want a healthy environment, be mindful of your purchases.

Finally, regarding sustainability in terms of "business ethics": I'm sorry to say but most luxury brands still use imported materials from sweatshops when they can definitely afford not to. Sure, the clothing may be made in countries with better working condition, but the material, itself, is usually going to be the same as those used in sweatshops. So, please, don't be deceived when you see a "Made in Italy" label thinking the entire product was made in Italy because that just means the product was manufactured in Italy; it does not mean the materials were from Italy. The only way to know for sure is if the company has transparency over its supply-side, which won't be the case for nearly all, if not all, large clothing companies, including luxury brands.

author: @JosMyOpinion
text:
When we try to address environmental concerns, we have to take a step back.

Fashion like this does an excellent job of targeting young women with trendy, and addictive, campaigns precisely because "feeling" good and "looking" good are a primary concern to many people.

A secondary concern is cost. Much like one woman said,  "why would I get that if I can get something else, cheaper?" Great question!

So, why? Well, when we explore environmental pollution in developing nations we always pay attention to the economic conditions of the people. If people do not earn substantial enough of a living to cover all costs and feel secure, they do not care about external factors that require activism.

The same can be said for young people. We know that they are aware of the environmental concerns and a potential climate crisis, but they can't see it. Simultaneously, their own resources are drained constantly by excessive costs in housing, living, childcare, transport, etc... So things that make them feel good become a priority at the lowest cost, rather than as an environmentally conscious choice.

To improve the environmental impact of fashion, we must first reduce the cost of living, or improve the economic conditions of the target markets, create supply chains that don't stop at the end user, but instead run all the way to the recycler, and most of all reduce the influence of marketing campaigns on the psyche of young people about what fashion actually means.

author: @anuna116
text:
In comment sections underneath shein shopping posts I often see heated arguments, usually with one side calling out people for not caring about the environment, and the other saying not to shame poor people/that there's class issues with buying more expensive sustainable clothes. And I agree that shopping truly sustainably and fairly is hard to attain for a lot of people, and also that realistically people still want to look cute and not buy one 100$+ piece of organic fair trade clothing a year. But it's the HAULS that are just so unnecessary and if you're spending 200$ on a haul every few months to get hundreds of shitty pieces you're going to wear 1-2 times in a season and you're still using the argument that you can't afford better things/the 'you're elitist/classist' defence, you should get a grip. Also the celebs. 
At least try to buy the pieces made of sturdier materials or natural materials, and learn to 'read' the cut to figure out how well it might sit and how practical it will be, and make sure to wash and dry everything properly. At least then they might last longer, and if they come apart, you could still recycle and make something new for yourself if it's cotton or linen, and if you do throw it away, it will not break apart into a zillion microplastics. I have cotton/linen zara/h&m pieces found on sale (in shein price range) that I've been wearing for 8-10 years now. It's doable to slowly change your wardrobe/habits and also thoughts - do you really need to keep up with a 52 week trend cycle? Who is it for? 
There IS a place in between 'i can't do anything about it anyway and why shouldn't i have more stuff' and 'i must be a perfect zero-waste vegan'. Everyone can start moving away from former towards the latter and it will be better to have millions of moderate people than a handful of perfect ones.

text:
I've heard of Shein, but have never shopped there. I'm not a fan of online clothes buying. The probabilities of the clothing not being the right size or color shown, and disappointment in quality of design and textiles used doesn't make the hassle worth it. Fast fashion is in theory is a lauded concept. In the sense that it generates a variety of choices for consumers. An amount of choices never seen before in consumerism. 

Colors, cuts, designs.... the world is full of endless possibilities. The direct downside of fast fashion though is that for the vast amount of clothing produced every year; what isn't sold has to go somewhere. And the very concept of 'easy buy-easy discard' has lead to a culture of disposal of unwanted goods as soon as they wear out or become unfashionable. And with quick turn-out companies like Shein that produce their products at such a high volume; the quality of those items isn't of the highest, most durable quality. So this creates a revolving and unsubstable system of unsold and discarded clothing being sold to vendors in 3rd world countries, and landing in waste dumps around the world.

Colors, cuts, designs.... the world is full of endless possibilities. The direct downside of fast fashion though is that for the vast amount of clothing produced every year; what isn't sold has to go somewhere. And the very concept of 'easy buy-easy discard' has lead to a culture of disposal of unwanted goods as soon as they wear out or become unfashionable. And with quick turn-out companies like Shein that produce their products at such a high volume; the quality of those items isn't of the highest, most durable quality. So this creates a revolving and unsubstable system of unsold and discarded clothing being sold to vendors in 3rd world countries, and landing in waste dumps around the world.

author: @studioghiblets958
text:
I am currently 24. For the last two years I’ve been changing the way I look at my clothes and fashion. I try to only buy clothes I absolutely am in love with and ones that I want in my wardrobe for the next foreseeable future but also ones that will last into that future. The sad thing with all the fast fashion clothing is that it is all synthetic fabrics. Some of the garments are quite cute and can trend for a while, but the low quality of the cheap synthetic materials will give before you have the piece for a year. I try to buy things made with a high or all cotton/linen fabric to help the longevity of my clothes, but that also means I have to be very conscious that this thick 100% cotton shirt may cost 50 dollars but that’s the price I have to pay if I want something that is hand made and sourced from good materials. 

I think for people my age, sometimes even including myself, it is hard to fully be aware of the future and also your impact on it. Plus is you’re making 12 an hour and have to pay rent, spending 50 dollars on a shirt is not possible or is only a rare splurge. It’s hard for a lot of people to see that, though I get 1 shirt for this much, it will last me the next 8 - 10 years and in the time I will slowly build up my collection of nice clothes which will also last a long time, saving me money in the long run. 

I think we need way more education not only from schools, teachers and influencers, but also parents need to step in and stop being so wasteful. Regardless on their opinion of climate change and global warming, everyone should just be teaching that things you own are precious and deserve respect. So many people in the generations above me have taught younger people that things are disposable: food, plastic cups, TVs, cloths, last year’s iphone. This kind of mentality is really ingrained and it’s really sad. 
If anyone is reading this essay I wrote, I challenge you to become more aware of things you’re unintentionally wasting. When you see people close to you doing those same thing, without acting superior or anything, call them out on it. The more we can become aware of our impact the better. 
Also in case this is news to you, recycling is the LAST RESORT in the recycle chain that you can do. 
I hope that if I live to my 40s the world hasn’t been drenched in flames as we work to get pollution towards extinction. I hope I can see you all in that world 🤍 

Be safe and live sustainably

Now everytime I order from there, I do think about how the worker's must not be getting paid well enough, and it can't really be sustainable/affordable to ship this internationally. But workers in America (including my household) don't get paid enough either, and for some reason, this Shein company is what working class Americans can afford. 

So until there are more affordable plus size stores available locally, they'll keep getting my business. And as I build my wealth, I hope to make and shop more handmade built-to-last fashion.

text:
I don't know. I almost felt pressure to buy from SHEIN because the pricing is just "too good", and I'm 32. 
But that was also the issue; while browsing I got more and more put off by the extremely low prices. The business model is completely unsustainable, except for those at the top exorbitantly benefiting from abusing the planet and its inhabitants to the max. 

I don't know if I could have "resisted", had I been a decade younger. 
Likely not, especially since I was still not only immature as well as impulsive (at that age, I had recently been diagnosed with ADHD, so unfortunately I went through my formative years without receiving much-needed treatment & support for my disability), but I was also very insecure in myself, combined with (still to this day) enjoying dressing up/"decorating myself". 
I also grew up in a single parent-household (after my other parent died in childhood), so my family was not financially well-off compared to my peers' here in Sweden. 
And I became legally an adult right around the global financial crash, which was followed by the European debt crisis. Fun times, I like toootally made it through unscathed without any mental health issues. 🙄 

So yeah: a variety of circumstances were already impacting me and influencing my purchasing decisions, despite growing up during the Internet's Wild West, and seeing my first smartphone in the summer of 2008. It was the heyday of blogging. Steam was massively improving and started to properly win people over. Spotify hadn't been launched yet then. I created this account when YouTube was still new—about 15 years ago. Twitter too was new. I felt like I was late getting on the Facebook train—joining in January 2008. Etc., etc., etc.

Today everything is just an invasive mass media onslaught: 
The relentless information overload, the unlimited 24/7 access and availability, the unconsensual aggressive molding & brainwashing of still-developing minds, the manipulative gamification pushing people towards gambling and other compulsive & addictive behaviours with the purpose of trapping them there, the problematically hypersexualized digital environments & extreme pornification of social media, and its excessive, intrusive, absolutely unavoidable content that saturates mainstream culture & disparately affects the every day life of young people within it. 
Humans who cannot protect nor defend themselves against this, because it happens regardless—everyone's an intended victim, nobody gets to shield themselves—and it does so without any regard to whether anyone actually ever intentionally seeks anything out. 
The sheer volume, the rampant consumerism, the exploitation, the forcible advertising shoved down our throats, the deeply disturbing objectification, the unwarranted pressure. 
The total disregard. 
The mental assault of it all. 
The unprecedented human experimentation on involuntary participants. 

I certainly would absolutely not like being a Gen Z:er today; I seriously don't know how they manage to cope. 😕

text:
I agree with your statements tbh. I never once followed trends ( might be because I’m lazy to) and what I have is fine. I never felt that  “I have nothing to wear feeling” though.

Why spend money and kill the environment at the same time just to ‘look cool’? 

I’m not saying it’s wrong to buy things or buy expensive branded things, but there’s a line that needs to be drawn. You have to asking yourself whether you actually need it? Needs before wants. Excessive spending and purchasing can only lead to unpleasant consequences. Take South Korea for an example, the household debt is growing by the second. There was a documentary done by CNA on it. And it points out how debt among young people has been steadily increasing. Either through bad spending habits or gambling, etc. But the documentary features two young people who explain why they spend so much. And the gist of it was like “to increase my self worth, that’s why I buy”.

This issue is a growing source of concern, over the not so transparent manufacturing of these ‘cheap’ fast fashion clothes , over the excessive spending of young people and over how companies like SHIEN are fueling and making use of this.

Moral of the story: buy only what you need when you need it. 
( and take all of that money you saved and put it into your retirement fund or savings, or try and save the world by donating to good causes , one dollar at a time)

author: @oldmckayla10
text:
If one does need a winter jacket or a shirt to replace their holey one, what if there are limited secondhand stores and/or no appropriate sizes? 


I'm the size of the average American woman, about a 1-2x or 18. I enjoy going to thrift stores, but most are a long drive away (more than hour one way), and the closest goodwill costs more than Walmart/Shein. 

IF they even have anything in my size. 95% of the time I've shopped for clothes in secondhand stores, there's nothing my size. Most women here do fall into that 1-2x, so my size tends to disappear first at Goodwill, Walmart, Kohls, etc (same with Large size Mens clothes too). 

I agree that kids really don't need to be wasting money on trendy clothes, and that buying secondhand is a better choice overall. But I don't think this video / these comments really address classism. 

They interviewed preppy college girls, not the poor rural people who have limited access to alternative stores. 

I'm privledged enough to get a day off and have limited access to a car that I could make a drive to big chain stores. But some of my neighbors don't even have access to that much, all they can get is limited delivery (like Shein/Amazon, not instacart/uber), and weekly carpool to the grocery stores / pharmacies. Lots of people don't have the time or ability to travel and sort through secondhand stores. 

Not to mention Facebook's algorithms and it being one of the few apps that works on low quality/speed internet. 

Some people do actually need clothes that fit, to replace the ones that are falling apart, and do have very limited options. Unfortunate Shein makes lower quality clothes that fall apart quickly, so it's like the Boots theory.

text:
Patagonia has the right idea and are sending a much-needed message, but it's not realistic to think that their way of manufacturing and selling clothes will provide sustainable clothing to the world. I say this as an ex-employee of Patagonia who still loves everything they do. That said, there are lots of things you can do to help even on a budget: 
A) buy second hand clothing. Of course there are thrift shops, yard sales, flea markets, 'vintage shops' and the like but also a growing number of online platforms for buying used clothes so it has never been easier. Every item received from someone else instead of pulled off a retail shelf is one item saved from the landfill and also one item not harming the environment again through production. Not to mention it's often cheaper (or gets you better quality than the same money in a retail shop). 
B) when buying new, don't go for the cheapest or on sale items, because those are often manufactured with bigger environmental impact, poorer worker conditions and worse durability. Carefully look at the garments you are considering, and if possible inspect them physically. You will often find there is a direct relation between durability (flimsy fabrics, poor stitching, quickly fading colours etc) and price, and this is truer the closer you get to the bottom end of the market. 
C) When buying clothes made of cotton, try to get organic if at all possible. Conventional cotton farming is one of the most polluting and environmentally taxing forms of agriculture in existence. Organic cotton farming isn't perfect but it's a lot better.
