author: @arghjayem
text:
It isn’t just about the landfill problem, which is a problem despite all the space we may seemingly have. Only natural textiles like silk, cotton, wool, cashmere, hemp etc. biodegrade- i.e. breakdown over time. Problem is most fashion items aren’t typically made with these materials, especially not the fast fashion items talked about in the video which tend to be lower quality materials because as the “fast fashion” moniker suggests, they need to be produced quickly and in quantity and go out of style equally quickly. 

So you tend to find more acrylics, polyesters and other man made materials being used on their own or in conjunction. Like t shirts where they are 80% cotton and 20% polyester because the polyester gives the shirt more elasticity and makes the fabric thinner. But even producing more natural materials is an issue. Take cotton, it is a natural material and will biodegrade, so it’s fine right? 

Wrong because as much as this video talks about the issue of the bulk production of fast fashion that is typically worn for less time than it took to produce before being thrown into landfill or recycled, there’s a bigger issue and that is the production. And not just production of the fashion items themselves in countries like Thailand where environmental protection isn’t as significant an issue as it is in the west, but also of the production of the raw material. 

Cotton, as I said before, may be biodegradable and less of a worry to throw out than a shirt made of acrylic or polyester which being plastic materials have as much an affect on the environment as plastic straws from Macdonalds, but the real issue with cotton is just the way we produce it and how we are producing it. It takes ALOT of water to maintain fields of cotton. So much that in the 1960’s in a effort to increase cotton production in the USSR, the Soviet government redirected 2 large rivers that originally fed into the Aral Sea in order to irrigate fields for cotton production in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan. The Aral Sea since then has become 10% of its original size and destroyed the fishing industries that once existed there. So it went from a body of Water equivalent in size to the states of West Virginia and Delaware, to one half the size of Connecticut. That is an issue. 

And going back to the production side, there are huge environmental issues there also. As I mentioned the environmental protection laws don’t exist or aren’t properly enforced in places like Thailand, Bangladesh etc where a lot of the worlds fast fashion is made. As well as being made of crappy materials and fabrics the dyes used are simply dumped into the local rivers on which factories are built. Which mean the rivers look more like the chemical vats that created the Joker in the Batman comics, unnaturally multicoloured frothy bodies of poison which the locals use as their only source of Water for washing themselves, their clothes and for drinking.

But this could all be fixed. We could buy less, invest more in what we wear. Focus on quality over quantity which would also mean we could repair or remake our clothes rather than simply chuck them out. There is so much the fashion industry could do to fix these issues but like every other industry we are still far too focused on the bottom line, until that changes we are doomed.

author: @itsalwayshalloweenexceptwh5118
text:
TLDR: the problem is the current culture around fashion, not the fact that women buy the most clothes for themselves and their children.

I want to weigh in with a more in depth opinion. Kevin Belcher is correct, mostly. For a little background; I did fashion school more than 10 years ago.
Most of the landfill of clothes will be women's and children's clothes.
At least for the last centuries women have been the ones that bought the most of the clothes for themselves and their families. This in itself is not a problem.

We've been having a problem with textile waste since the 80's at least. The problems here are how quickly trends shift, the quality of the clothes being produced, the lifespan of the clothes, the amount of clothes being produced vs the amount of those clothes being bought, a change in the culture of thrift/re-use/mend.

For example let's take the 1950's; people didn't have as many clothes in their wardrobe as people do now, making your own clothes was very commonplace, the quality of clothes sold was much higher (and so was the lifespan if taken care of correctly) and so was the price. I don't know about second hand stores in the 50's, but I do know it was common to have "hand me downs" even outside of poor families.
People who were especially thrifty reused items of clothes by taking all the seams apart, ironing the pieces, and using the fabric to sew a new item.
People also knitted and crocheted more items that they could use.
If something was broken they tried to mend it, like replacing a lining or darning a sock.
Another bit of information is that it was the standard back then that the item such as a dress or blouse, was produced in the same country it was sold in.

Clothing is able to be produced much cheaper now, quality can be so poor the item such as a t-shirt may fall apart in the first wash. There are a lot of shady practices in the garment industry (bangladesh, india, china etc), think of "sweat shops".
I don't know why or when it came about but it's like the fashion industry decided we no longer have 4 seasons, we now have 52. That means a new trend every week.
It's the fashion industry who is making those trends. And people who suffer from FOMO (fear of missing out) or a desire to be on trend will want to buy those trends. 
Most of these people are teenage girls and young adult women, which means they want these trends to be affordable for them.
The idea being that a teenager with an after school job should be able to afford a few items of clothing each month.
And that's where places like H&M and Primark step in. They items are cheap and don't have a long lifespan, and they don't have to be because after a few months the item is no longer in trend. These are not timeless items, they are dated.

Because of these shifts in the industry more expansive brands can get away with selling poor quality items for a high price. In fashion you do not always get what you pay for.
It can be quite difficult to find a brand with the right quality for price ratio.

My advice to reduce the waste; find a brand that produces clothes that last and that have timeless pieces, stick with them, don't buy too much.
Re-evaluate the contents of your wardrobe every year, if there are items you haven't worn the entire year either plan to wear them and stick to that plan, or donate them to a thrift shop.

Better yet, go thrifting yourself. Bonus points; learn how to make your own clothes.

Over 80% of my casual clothes are thrifted, over 90% of my formal clothes are home made.

⁠@seanea5663things that are made from natural fibers are a good start - and be sure to check the percentages. author: @CourtneyCoulson
text:
For centuries most people wore maybe a dozen outfits in their entire lives. Now we wear a new outfit everyday. 
I have bought from op shops for years, but it still left me with a massive wardrobe and I only wore maybe 5% of those garments regularly.
Here's my new approach:
1. Make my own clothes, which is what people used to do in the first half of the 20th century. 
2. Never impulse buy. If I see something I like, I will walk away and if I'm still thinking about it later in the week, I will get it. 
3. Pick a colour palette. I never have to stress about colour coordination or having those random items that don't go with anything. I mostly just wear green, with purple, pink and red in the minority.
4. Buy organic and ethically sources where possible. 
5. Buy things that last. It might seem like a big cost upfront, but it's worth it.

author: @marietailor3100
text:
I think we’ve got a few problems here:
1. We broke. No matter how you play it, if you need a tank top or a t-shirt and you don’t have one, buying one from a fast fashion shop is probably going to be the easiest thing for you to do. (This is especially true if you’re a person whose body type isn’t strictly “average”).
2. Even if you can afford to buy something nicer/better quality, it’s hard to tell what is and isn’t good. For example, some things at H&M and at Zara are durable. But let’s be real - Zara ISNT EVEN CHEAP! So when you’re trying to figure out what’s over-priced brand-based luxury and what’s good quality, you kind of just shrug.
3. The internet makes it EVEN HARDER to know when you’re buying fast fashion and when you’re not. With the death of malls, a lot of us have to go online when we’re looking for something we need. But then there are all these sites you may or may not have heard of that have various brands listed on them. Are those in-house brands? Unclear. Some of these fast-fashion sites try to trick you into believing the quality isn’t terrible by charging more than they need to. 

My point is, I can’t blame consumers for this one. It’s too complicated and impractical to really get a sense of what actual prices should be and what they can expect. Moreover, while “fashion” isn’t a need, clothes are. And everyone’s favourite solution of thrifting can be deeply impractical for lots of groups of people - ex. those with allergies esp. pet allergies; people who need a specific clothing item (do they have a  button down dress shirt in you size that will work with your uniform?); people who don’t have cars (in my experience, you have to be able to go to 8 thrift stores in a day to make it work. The bus is not great for that); finding similar items for different people; and so on. 

This issue to me is a classic regulatory one. It’s not one that can or should be reasonably solved by consumers but needs to be solved by governments since industry wont do it on its own.

author: @Avantime
text:
Planned obsolescence is not a new thing at all, there has always been low-quality clothing more akin to rags. The thing is that back then even rags can be expensive because it's often inefficiently made and sold at local shops at a huge markup, and as a result both men and women had to learn sewing to patch their torn clothing. It's just that with globalization things got real cheap, and with that comes more spending power. America is a consumer economy, if the consumer doesn't spend, the economy suffers disproportionally. The country hardly exports anything but (potentially dangerous) Boeing jets, corn and natural gas.

The key is not to buy quality stuff for life, it's buying the quality you need for your use case, and no more. For example in 3:50, a $3 vs. $80 sweater - I can buy 26 of the $3 sweater before I hit $80, and let's say a $80 sweater lasts 10 years. With the $3 sweater I can keep buying the same sweater every 5 months for the next 10 years, and if that $3 sweater lasts more than 5 months, I'm financially ahead. This is especially true for lesser worn items in the wardrobe - if I only wear it 10 times a year a $3 sweater can last years.

This reminds me of the uninsured farmer laughing at his flood-destroyed crop. The other guy say "Why are you laughing?" and he replies "Well the loss of this crop costs me less than what I would've paid for in insurance over the years, so I'm financially ahead!"

author: @soup983
text:
This video implies many inaccurate aspects of the global fashion industry and spreads misinformation in itself, which it's trying to debunk. 

I feel like the producers behind this video need to understand that just because something is made outside of North America does not mean it is made unethically or their labour is being exploited and "not paid a living wage," and presuming so if viewing the world in a very "Ameri-centric, western-centric" POV. 

More research should've been done before creating this video, as Temu, which is the Western version of an extremely large Chinese company "Pinduoduo," which manufactures most of their items inside China, allowing for cheap costs and labour, but just because it is inexpensive, doesn't mean its unethical. 

China's manufacturing ability, especially in clothing, is at the world's top. Living costs are low, and statistics show that 95% of people working in factories in the clothing sector in China are paid ethically and fairly. So, if you buy from Temu, you're likely to spend your money paying for something other than sweatshop labour, but rather the skilled labour of skilled workers from China. 

Suppose you buy from a slightly affordable "slow-fashion" brand. In that case, they are most likely manufacturing in China in the same factories that Temu shop owners source from since many designs and patterns can only be made on machines invented explicitly in China by Chinese manufacturers. text:
Mickey Mouse Clubhouse might look silly and harmless, but if you think about it like a sci-fi or comic book fan, it can absolutely be framed as one of the most powerful “weapons” in the universe. Here’s why:

⸻

1. Infinite Adaptability
	•	The Mousketool always provides the exact tool Mickey needs for any situation, no matter how specific or improbable. That’s basically reality-bending—it means the Mousketool can manifest anything.
	•	In power-scaling terms, that’s like having a weapon that changes form and function instantly to counter any threat.

⸻

2. Predictive Intelligence
	•	The Mousketool doesn’t just give random objects—it somehow knows ahead of time which tools will be useful later.
	•	That makes it a mix of probability manipulation, precognition, and tactical support rolled into one. Imagine a weapon that already knows the enemy’s weakness before the fight begins.

⸻

3. Cartoon Physics
	•	Since it’s from a toon universe, the Mousketool doesn’t obey normal laws of physics. A balloon might carry a castle, or a rope might stretch infinitely. That makes it basically unstoppable by normal means.
	•	If it follows cartoon logic, it can outmatch even “serious” weapons like lightsabers or Infinity Stones, because it plays by a different ruleset.

⸻

4. Universal Accessibility
	•	Anyone can use it. The Mousketool responds to whoever asks for help, which means it’s not limited to one wielder. That universality makes it a force-multiplier—like if everyone in your army had a reality-warping artifact in their pocket.

⸻

5. Non-violent but Omnipotent
	•	Unlike traditional weapons, it’s designed for problem-solving, not destruction. That means it can disarm or neutralize threats without collateral damage. A tool that can solve any problem peacefully is arguably more dangerous than one that can just blow things up.

⸻

6. Potential for Cosmic Scale
	•	If the Mousketool can conjure anything, in theory it could generate:
	•	A black hole in a box
	•	An antidote to any poison
	•	A key to lock away galactic tyrants
	•	Or even another Mousketool (infinite recursion)

That’s basically omnipotence disguised as a children’s cartoon gimmick.

⸻

So, in nerd terms:
👉 The Mousketool is like if the Green Lantern Ring, the Infinity Gauntlet, and Bugs Bunny’s cartoon logic had a baby.

text:
Look at how AI prompts are turned into motion videos: text symbol-image-sequence-movement. A prompt becomes form, form becomes motion.

That’s the same process happening in what you call “physical” reality. Thought- symbol -pattern- experience- movement. The prompt is awareness itself. Reality is just the rendered output.

When you watch an AI video, you’re seeing a mirror of how this place actually works. Prompts generate frames, frames stitched together give the illusion of continuity but it’s all arising from the same underlying motion.

The difference is scale, not function.

The ego can’t control this, because the ego isn’t the one prompting.

text:
The commercial was so obviously meant to be controversial. Just like the Schick razor commercial a couple years ago, and multiple other commercials over the last several years: companies want to play upon culture war politics in their ads, bc any major publicity is seen as beneficial to their next quarterly earnings. It obviously doesn’t always work that way, sometimes it leads to a loss next quarter, etc, but most cases of this that I can remember over the last few years, it’s been a success. Then only a few months later, most of the time, most people move on. 

That’s all the ad was. American Eagle aren’t white supremacist, just like Schick absolutely could not have given a flying fork about toxic masculinity, just like none of these corporations are ever actually feminist. People who do advertising in these companies have known for decades how easy to manipulate the average person is, and so sometimes that’s exactly what they seek to do in advertising. I’ve honestly wondered if people writing think pieces on this stuff are paid by the companies responsible for the drama. Whatever the case, these are all major corporations and/or part of conglomerates that almost always have a fiduciary responsibility to shareholders to maximize profits, thus are legally obliged to advertise in ways they find to accomplish those ends. That’s what this is, and any actual overlap in values with those working for the companies are incidental at best.

Oh, and I totally agree with the winner omg I love Gap yasss!

💫storytime💫 : it's a well known fact that hot topic managers are some of the worst people to ever work in retail - years ago, I had a hot topic manager (exact same stereotype that hunter described) deny my use of a hot topic gift card because, and I quote, "you didn't sign the back before entering the store". in no world does anyone need to sign the back of a gift card to use it lmao it's not a check 🤦‍♀️ I would know, I managed a massive retail store for 4 years before I went to college. author: @paranoah1925
text:
Thanks for making such a nuanced video on fast fashion. Most videos barely scratch the surface.

I can't comment on other 'developed' countries, but in American society depression, overconsumption, narcissism, isolation, wealth-envy, social media, materialistic behaviour, hyper-individualism and the distorted idea of success are all linked and feed off each other. What we fail to notice is that the over-consumption is not even positively related to overall life satisfaction. 

The root of all of the things i listed above is the ego. The ego makes us compare ourselves to each other and when in this comparison we find ourselves lacking, the ego can make us depressed. The same ego makes us narcissistic and think we deserve more than others and at the cost of others. This is why anything that quietens the default mode network (DMN), like meditation, neuro-feedback or psychedelics, alleviates depression and makes us feel connected to others. DMN is sort of the seat of the ego.

This is why the people who fall for the rat race are unlikely to respond to moralistic arguments like exploitation of people in poorer countries and respond with their own twisted moralistic judgements. The ego just wants us to be perceived as good (or successful or intelligent or capable), the ego doesn't care about the truth.

We should encourage people to travel east, experience different cultures, meet different people, spend time in nature and explore Eastern philosophy (or eastern spirituality as the west calls it. I am not talking about the religious stuff, but the real philosophy and techniques which developed over years of debate and lived experience of real yogis/monks etc). While you are at it, also learn about medicine (rather, health and well-being) from an eastern point of view. It has a lot to offer.

text:
American overconsumption is like the hungry ghosts in the cycle of life. There is insatiable desire and any attempt to meet these desires just leads to more suffering and even greater desire. And corporations are using the best and latest findings in human psychology to exploit vulnerabilities and trap people in the realm of the hungry ghost. 

"According to Yangsi Rinpoche, the suffering of the beings born in the realm of the hungry ghosts is far more intense than those born in the animal realm."
(The animal realm is characterised by creatures driven by impulse and instinct. The difference, however, is that their needs and desires can be fulfilled and they are not trapped in the endless cycle of ever increasing cravings.)

The good news is that we can break out of the hungry ghost realm and make ourselves immune to the manipulations of these corporations and their marketing. The place to start would be to look within and search for true contentment.

author: @FelisImpurrator
text_clean: @Peridot-banana In a very real sense, much of this impulse to seek purity seems to stem from a sort of internalized trauma people inherit from (quite specifically) socially conservative upbringing. The idea of self-flagellating asceticism as a form of purification seems to be hand in hand with hierarchical conservative ideology - fear of the unknown manifesting as a desire to render things controlled and predictable, often by punishing that which falls out of line. By imposing Order upon oneself through self-denial, one may reclaim a semblance of control over the chaotic and confusing outside world. Even people who consider themselves progressive often internalize such mindsets, and more or less manifest the core behaviors even as they're reframed in the aesthetics of radical change. At the end of the day systemic problems require systemic solutions, not the cultivation of a personal sense of virtue.

text:
@FelisImpurrator Ab-so-lutely. I have thought about this a lot and how it is rooted in the conjoining of Christian ideology and prison/disposability culture. Because we have the pervasive notion that our goodness is ultimately centered on individual internal correctness, only observable by an objective and all-seeing deity.  Failure of this internal goodness ultimately means being deemed bad and cast away into hell. We reproduce this dynamic in prison culture, with "rehabilitation" supposedly being the punishment (penance) that is supposed to reform a person internally so they can be worthy of engagement with community again, otherwise, they deserve to be cast out and treated as disposable and only fit for more punishment.
The thought patterns that arise from this moral system are completely unavoidable, no matter how much we may not accept Christian ideology or prison culture. We have to be actively working to reject those notions of individual purity and disposability and building alternative visions of community morality, not just creating new iterations of the same rigid moral configurations, where only the ways to "deserve heaven" shift.

author: @hirokoai3013
text:
One of the main problem I experienced, as a student from the Global North, is the mental implications behind the material questions. Trying to consume a bit more responsibly is very, very mind consuming. Every piece of fabric, every food item, has a flaw, depends on the exploitation of someone (from the South as the North by the way, I've heared too much stories of cultivators actually losing money by working), has some shady environmental pratice. Even more "responsible" brands often uses the same methods of exploitation and clean their image by, for example, delegating their production, it justifies a higher price. It takes lots of knowledge to navigate between this, it would take literally months to be able to chose responsible products. Aside from this you may have long work hours, some fatigue, family problems, health concerns, everydaylife things to arrange and you add the responsibility to tackle with those complex social and environmental issues, it can rapidly become soul crushing. It happened several time for me to be in the supermarket (for example), to ask what I can by, to imagine what it implies, and at a moment, completely tired, I simply say myself "screw this world". Those are collective problems, these should be adressed with collective decisions. It is completely unfair from those who own the capital, who exploits people from the global south and leave employee from the global North unemployed because they were not willing to pay for decent working conditions, to let their responsibilities on the shoulders of people who are not professionals and who actually have a life.

My best fast realistic advices to most people :
- Do not feel guilty, this situation is not your fault. Breethe a bit, try to enjoy your life a bit.
- Try the best you can to make things better, but stay afloat. All the easy things you can try, but make sure you understand what you are doing before, companies are good at manipulating people. And you deserve good quality stuff.
- For your consumption, plan on the long run. Think to what you really want in the next decades. And take care of you materials. It is a good way to use your money into less exploiting, better quality, more durable stuff.

For long-termism, in the specific example of fashion, you will probably never be normal enough for the society, try to develop a several years, or even decades plan about the esthetics you want to develop. Your goal is not to be in the trend, but to stand out, it is a strategy of "charisma over trend", this way, you won't be outdated anytime soon and you will be able to slowly develop a style, and to use high quality clothes for years, and good jewelry for decades.

author: @poiseblemiramoon6992
text:
A big undertone in this argument, is still that participating  in such capitalist system of core exploiting the periphery in fast fashion, is something that participants in the global north should feel bad, alarmed or guilt, and that they should be stopped. Even though you did hint that the power of the system, though downplayed, is more powerful than the person, i find that this online argument is still centered around the person by virtue of the exchanges online being literally inter-personal. We are persons that empathise with persons; it is easier to think, and to start thinking, in terms of person as opposed to system. How to thus make this argument be effective needs to make a statement on explicitly why the person needs to feel so personally involved that they should take personal action such as stop overconsuming. For a cosmopolitan audience, this is easy. 

But this is a privileged position. Not everyone is cosmopolitan, and at present moment, not everyone has the mind and energy, to feel the obligation to care for the other that they might be indirectly oppressing that are thousands of miles away, by virtue of living in a system. My family in the more impoverished areas of Jiangxi, China, would more think of how to save budget in spending for clothes from fast-fashion-like products in wholesale markets, and that is a priority over thinking about what system they live in and to act. And I still think what they choose to do would at least be correct for their situation.

Critical thinking, cosmopolitan thinking, thinking of the ‘other’, is still nascent across the population. And we fall into a paradox where when we produce such videos of cosmopolitan arguments we inevitably direct it to a cosmopolitan audience- thus preaching to the choir. The fact that we use English, a global north language, the more major language of some new Gen Zs that think more of the world, indirectly maintains this paradox. We have a long way to go. 

Saying fast fashion is bad (although it is)- not many people would have or feel the obligation to care and put this to a high enough priority to act. We are persons in and of ourselves and its not intuitive to want to think of the “far-away other” under a global capitalist system

author: @lemonlin1627
text: I think part of the additional difficulty across all socio-economic backgrounds, but especially for lower classes, is the time and mental load to distinguish sustainable from fast fashion. It’s not just a higher price tag, many companies that parade as high end or haute couture still use the same sweat shops and mass production systems as h&m or zara. There’s a level of time commitment, research, and fashion literacy to cut through the bullshit and understand the true quality of a product, especially with online purchases when you can’t look at the product in person and images can be photoshopped or referencing an entirely different product than what’s being sold. Falsified reviews, taking down negative reviews, advertising through sponsored tiktoks that are not tagged or labeled properly, using multiple brand names with different identities that trace back to the same company, and other similar tactics all make it as hard as possible for a consumer to understand what to buy. If anyone has resources or recommendations for sustainable brands or collections for clothing and more (consumables, food, toiletries and cosmetics, etc) please let me know! I want to be more considerate in my spending and enjoy long lasting, high quality product but I get bogged down in the slog through a very difficult consumer landscape.

text:
OOOOH I wish we could reach through the screen sometimes and give some commenters a slap. Socialist Mommy is completely obfuscating the argument. First of all, the percentage of the population who live in impoverished areas where second-hand clothing stores are rare is likely a smaller number than the percentage of people who DO have access to affordable second-hand clothing, and choose NOT to buy from there, but instead from fast fashion brands. Secondly, the brainwashing of the fashion industry towards the consumer that they need to buy an excessive amount of clothing to "feel good" is PART OF THE PROBLEM. It's keeping people in debt, stopping them from taking meaningful and healthy steps towards supporting their mental health, and PROMOTING classism. It's how we end up with women being looked down upon for wearing the same outfit twice. 

Socialist Mommy is 100% a fast fashion consumer who is wilfully engaging in cognitive dissonance to absolve her of guilt, as are all the little trolls upvoting her. Don't get me wrong, I'm not perfect. I eat meat. I have struggled between feelings of guilt, and the desire not to change, for a loooong time. It's easy to make excuses to avoid quitting meat- "I'm a picky eater and don't want to restrict further", "but I do enough for the environment already, people shouldn't judge me!" or "it wouldn't make a difference if I quit meat, the meat industry is massive!" are all thoughts that have brought me comfort, but in the end they are rubbish. I just don't want to quit. I'm selfish in that respect, and that's uncomfortable and makes me feel guilty. So to summarise, Socialist Mommy, shut your face. You might have a bunch of people fooled with your rhetorical nonsense, but not me.

author: @VWYL900802
text:
I have a cousin that’s close to my mom’s age, her mom, my aunt, my other aunt, and many others were part of the 60-70s factory age in HK. My cousin ended up going to China to continue to do factory work to feed her family, these women didn’t get a chance to go to school. They left school at the age of 12. In HK education is the way out, it meant life will be different, so quitting school to be a factory girl because your own family can’t make ends meet, and you have a lot of siblings in a 100 square feet housing in the projects, sacrifices for the sake of family had to be made. My cousin started to change her life when she started to learn yoga and actually went to India to learn yoga and became a yoga instructor in HK for years, she quit her job as a factory worker at 55, over the years in her youth, her mom did the overbearing mom pressuring her to get married and she just never got time. She worked for long hours for years. She decided eventually to not get married and just focus on yoga. For many people who worked in the factories, that life was all they have, leaving it, they can’t survive, their education is too minimal. This is a systemic issue. 
My dad knew how factory system works in China. He’s not related, those women are from my mom’s side, he’s just from China, particularly the south. Honestly, people there don’t care about your tiny charities. It just won’t get to there. It gets to the country’s respective charity organizations, but it doesn’t change the whole landscape the society problems enough to actually help the factory workers. Not even a charity luncheon could get there. The real change is change from within. This really is about oppression needing to realize they need to leave oppression in their own way. It’s really is about ignorant Regan era west willing to do business with oppressive China and unknowingly helping animal farm China enslave naive and rural Chinese, who are willing because they can escape hardwork in backwards hard farming life. No matter what, once they leave rural life, with such lack of education and lack of resources, will end in extreme class exploitation, either in prostitution, or factory slavery. No matter what, it won’t change the corruption from within. And when technology becomes too advanced, these people will have to go above and beyond to catch up, with no space for actual self improvement or enrichment. So it’s materialistic gains for the sake of materialistic gains to save face for your backwards parents in rural China. It’s now overwhelmingly materialistic, with no real understanding about humanism. They know humanity, and realism in the most practical sense, but no real humanism. This is why now the downfall of China we see now. 
I left HK when I was 3 and grew up in Canada. I never really knew about the slavery and factory in China and how it relates to me growing up, every time my mom talked about it, I just thought it lame and annoying. When I knew about it and the lengths of severity it really is, my cousins and people in the community told their stories, to me these people knew and don’t care because they accepted their destiny. We are all one people and when you left for a better life, you worked really hard to get there and you can be that lucky, that’s your destiny. For me personally, I find the paradox of this makes me feel ironic because I’m buying clothes that could be made by my people coming from an oppressive life, it’s a different life and different destiny. White people don’t pander, don’t pity. If you really want to make a difference, help oppressive countries choose not to be oppressive. If you believe that you can’t force people change their mind, then, let’s see how current world issues unfolds.

text:
I've seen and participated in many conversations about this and while I do believe some arguments ARE classist (meaning some arguments people make about this subject are classist), I don't think saying fast fashion is harmful and bad IS classist. We are all responsible for reducing harm to both each other AND to the environment and fast fashion harms people and the planet. 

When I was younger, there was this simple idea... if you couldn't afford it, you couldn't have it. And that meant, yes, sometimes I wore clothes that weren't trendy, nice, or even in good shape. We didn't have a thrift store so I had to rely on my clothes to last. I had to learn how to sew holes, to patch, to be clever. I remember wearing plastic bags in my boots in the winter to stop my feet from getting wet because the boots couldn't keep the wet out on their own anymore. We made it work. 

Just because you don't have access to thrift stores and resources for free/cheap clothes, doesn't mean you're entitled to HARM others just to 'look good'. Appearance means nothing. How you look means nothing. What you do means everything.

It is not classist to say: Hey, if you can't afford it, you can't have it. Especially in regards to superficial things like clothes.

It would be classist to say: You're too poor to EVER have a Louis Vuitton bag so we're going to CUT UP AND DESTROY every bag that doesn't sell so that those nasty poor people won't ever be able to touch these ONLY FOR RICH PEOPLE bags. That's classist.

Anyway. I don't think I'm adding much to the conversation... just wanted to leave a comment really.

author: @MaddHattrix
text:
There is complexity with the "fast fashion" debate, which is why no one ever wins on either side of the debate truly. While on one hand, fast fashion is bad for the environment, has been known to exploit workers for low wages, and is usually of a low quality, many of those making arguments against fast fashion are in a privileged position where they CAN question the morality of affordable brands. Everyone wants to point out the problem, but their solutions are short-sighted and often coming from people in middle class lifestyles. It's nice and dandy to shop at some ethical fashion store online, but the higher quality and ethically sound products tend to go for higher prices, as they have to in order to beat inflation. High quality materials cost more to make, and handmade items are charged higher for the quality of the time and work, too. The problem stems from privileged people condemning those who buy cheaper fast fashion options without offering other ethical and affordable alternatives. There can't be headway in the conversation until that happens. 

Second hand fashion isn't always the solution either. 1) Second hand stores don't offer enough variety, especially when it comes to sizes 2) Not all donation and charity shops, like Salvation Army, are as clean and sanitized as one would hope. Some people literally dump junk there. I volunteered at one of the Salvation Army shops and it was horrible what was "donated". 3) These aren't always available in every community. The pull of fast fashion is people who don't have transportation, both personal and public in their area, can order fast fashion online because of their wider distribution practices. People confined to their homes can access it. Local thrift and donation shops don't yet offer that accessibility much yet. 4) Second-hand fashion needs to be replenished, which creates a cycle of buying. We can't all shop thrift if we expect it to be less wasteful.

Now, yes, there are elite wealthy people purchasing fast fashion outfits every week so they can get a new look for social media. That happens. But even for them, it wouldn't happen as frequently if there were affordable and accessible yet ethically sound options out there. For some, that's an investment in outfits for social media, an investment in a future career in entertainment, possibly to make money. 

We also have to understand where fast fashion began and why so many business owners fall victim to it, which is another angle most people don't think about. There are people interested in designing in the fashion industry, and many want to be ethical, but the cost to buy materials, create, and distribute becomes high, especially when you don't come from a wealthy background. I watch Youtubers of people starting their own boutiques and fashion businesses from the ground up. The problem they always run into is meeting the fast demands of the public, trying to make a certain amount of money to pay their bills, while maintaining quality and an ethical method of mass producing. That balance isn't easy to master and can't be talked down with a "Don't buy fast fashion" speech. It needs to be addressed from a deeper angle in order to rid the industry of fast fashion.

Exploitation of workers, Exploitation of lands and materials; companies continue to do this because no overseeing entities exist to stop them. And we like to pretend as the nations in which these workers are exploited hold no responsibility to protect their citizens. Nations in the global north can start creating stricter standards about what sells there but I'm not sure how much they can influence the quality of life for citizens in the global south. We can try our best but the solution needs to come from these countries as well. They must balance industrial and economic growth with the interest of their people as well. Countries in global north alreqdy went through many of these trial and errors during industrialization.

author: @DiscontentKiwi
text:
Also one shouldn't forget the lack of larger sizes in stores as well as thrift stores. Larger size people already suffer from fat phobia in society, and when we then get the rare opportunity to buy modern clothes in OUR size, to a price that we can actually afford (I don't care that the jeans costing 400 USD last longer, I CAN'T pay it). Like, we can either go naked, wear ill fitting clothes and get flak for that, wear well fitting but ugly clothes and get flak for that while most likely also get poor buying them, OR buy fast fashion and get to participate in society. 🤷 Like a lot of people in the comments point out, it's also not about buying HUGE amounts ever month. I mean, I buy a pair of 15 USD jeans maybe every six months.

Also remember, hauls on YouTube can be very useful to work against over consumption, especially from plus size people; having ONE person buy a bunch, try them out and show them to the rest of us, very well prevents us buying a bunch of shit we won't like or can't wear.

I think it's very important to point out flaws in industries, and the things we can do, and of course recognize that other groups of people suffer from it, and try to prevent it. But it's also important to recognise that being born in the West doesn't come with all the privileges you might think, and it's wrong to shame individuals for doing what they can to survive in a classist, patriarchal, fat phobic society.

To be clear; I'd LOVE to buy local, sustainable, female and black owned, organic and well made things, OR thrift my entire wardrobe. But I can't afford it, and neither those small businesses nor the thrift stores carry my sizes. So, excuse me while trying to lead a decent life, while trying to work against non sustainable practices in other ways.

Fast fashion is another one of those astonishingly horrible practices that were allowed to flourish in our globalist systems. The promise was cheap clothing for everyone and saving time by not having to make your own clothes anymore.
The reality is brutally horrendous working conditions out of the western sight, making cheap quality clothing that is horribly cut with awful feels that legit falls apart after two weeks of use (if you're lucky). In the end you end up having to buy clothing 4 times more often than if you initially spent significantly more for an actual quality product that lasts you a while. (Prize =/= Quality of course, but it can be an indicator.) In the end you save money by buying quality over quantity. 
The initial investment might not be something everybody can do on a whim (I couldn't either), but over the course of a couple of years you can switch things out, buying second hand, or go shopping at the start of the month.
That is not even speaking about the insane amounts of water, agricultural area and labor force being wasted for a pile of produced waste that you couldn't even fathom if you tried, or the pointless seasonal fashion trends that the industry has cracked itself into.

text:
Due to the fact that a lot of fast fashion is cheaply made in sweatshops (therefore wont protect you from certain weather conditions or be comfortable), I would recommend someone to who is lower income to possibly save up and buy something that will last longer and will have an overall better garment to wear, perhaps in colder weather (for example: a thick winter coat instead of an assortment of "cute" jackets from shein). Of course, I also am aware that this is not an option for everyone who is in immediate need of clothes. Though, even if some of these brands have higher prices (typically higher price should mean better quality), they STILL have their clothing made in sweatshops. While yes, the clothing IS still better quality and *much* better than clothing from shein or forever 21, its still being produced in a sweatshop. It seems like the only place to get clothing that doesnt encourage underpayed laboring is purchasing second hand or thrifting. But with goodwill beginning to raise their prices, salvation army being homophobic (thus donating to anti-lgbt organizations), and local thrifts not being as popular or have as many clothes, it seems impossible to find any trendy clothing able to match everyones style. So heres my recommendation: Try to purchase second hand if you can, it should always be the first option but if you are unable to access it, the *very occasional* purchase from a non-secondary/fast fashion brand is (not ideal, but) acceptable. Though, dont purchase too many garments (even from secondhand, overconsumption is in every corner of the fashion industry). Simply buy what you need or you are certain you will be wearing often and comfortably. 

p.s - if you are financially stable enough to support (and arent finding anything interesting from thrifts), try to find some small clothing businesses to buy from who cater to your specific style!

Ugh, a lot of debunked socialist "thought" that wants to lump every evil in the world into one neat and false explanation of literally every ill of civilization. Sorry folks, but this entire premise just doesn't make sense. Say the "Global North" left the "Global South" alone and didn't colonize at all. A group of countries, through sheer luck, ended up at the crossroads of a variety of technological developments at just the right time in history for them to take advantage of all that technology. Ok, that means that a fluke of technological development gave them their advantages, not colonialism. Colonialism was a byproduct of a few nations having massively better guns than everyone else for long enough to take over. That's it. 

Reversing this would not fundamentally alter the situation in any way. It would just be a different group of countries having massively better guns and taking over.

text: I think a big part of “there’s no ethical consumption under capitalism” in youth generations is also part of the emotional fatigue. A lot of kids these days grow up being absolutely soaked in suffering and guilt that’s not their responsibility, and it’s definitely gotten more intense over the years. We are asking these kids to accept their terrible inheritance of a doomed world in a way previous generations have not had to, and to be the ones to change and fix it. Sometimes, people just want to exist and not be made to feel guilty for existing. So it’s often being used as kind of a shorthand for “I didn’t ask for this existence and I am tired of being made to feel guilty for anything I find enjoyment from due to the inequitable systems that we exist in that were set up far before my existence began and to which I truly have no power over.” While it’s a limited and privileged take, it’s not necessarily incorrect. I agree that people in the Global North should do better, it is hard to convince someone that is so overwhelmed with suffering coming from multiple different angles in a more aggressive way than ever seen before that they should take the time to individually be more ethical and feel more guilty about wanting a cute top.

author: @nihilism1652
text:
Hello! Certified person from the global south, especially from South Asia. Not India or Bangladesh, but their third sibling, Pakistan. Firstly I wanted to thank you for taking out the time to not only talk about the exploitation of the global south in terms of fast fashion but also referencing actual scholars, especially people like Spivak who don’t have a colonized and imperial view of our countries because God knows just about everyone and every piece of media does. I wanted to share some things as someone who has spent their entire 24 years of existence in Pakistan. 

Firstly, I know that no one here actually knows anything about Pakistan because no one in the global north talks about Pakistan in such discussions, so let me tell you something fascinating: the biggest industry in Pakistan, like other third world countries, is textile. I had absolutely no idea about fast fashion before like 2019 because it’s not something that exists in my country. Over here store bought stitched clothes aren’t nearly as popular as buying unstitched clothes and having them stitched by tailors, which is much cheaper in comparison and just generally eliminates fitting and style problems. The only distinction between clothes is that there are normal shops and then there are branded stores like Khaadi and Sana Safinaz, that are designer and local. We don’t have any Zara etc here. In fact we only started properly importing luxury items some time in the 2010s. When I was a kid we only had one local brand of potato chips and juice. Normal people wear non designer clothes and rich people wear designer clothes. Everything is local, but that’s also because we literally manufacture clothes on an international scale. 

My dad is in the textile business as well. He has a modest company and we’re not rich but we live comfortably. Because of him I know about how the textile industry here works, and the way in which the cloth is exported to the global north. It is something seen as ironic here that clothes that are manufactured here cost twice as much when imported in the form of stitched clothes. The cloth to make the shirt is say $1, but after being stitched by some western company they cost say $3, which is already over twice the initial cost. It’s a weird scam we fall into when we buy western clothes here, from stores that are branded. It’s funny because we can buy the same kind of shirt from a small market for half the price, but most people don’t because of status. I don’t know if the clothes sold here (I’ve been talking about our desi kind of clothes this entire time) have the same kind of shelf life as fast fashion stuff but we wear the same clothes regularly for years, and as someone else in the comments said, they go through the cycle of becoming home clothes and then dusters. The way in which the global north wastes things is beyond me. 

Tldr; I’m Pakistani, which is global south, our entire economy is based on exporting cloth to global north countries and we’re paid very little for it. Thank you for talking about our exploitation properly and in detail. The entitlement of most global north citizens astounds me. They can’t even begin to imagine how things are for people who are working class in my country, or India and Bangladesh, or any other country in the global south. It’s crazy how unaware, ignorant and out of touch they are with what happens in third world countries and how they continue to add to it.

The ideology of Liberalism is ultimately based in minarchism, democratic republic, civil rights, and Capitalism. The ideology first came in the Enlightenment Era, and which was once promoted as a humble alternative to absolute monarchies became something that fueled many revolutions.

However with revolutions, comes contradictions, and many proponents of Liberal democracies attempted to correct these contradictions. On one hand you have Keynes and John Stuart Mill. Neither Classical Liberals nor Socialists, but in between. These Liberals saw the real problems with unregulated capitalism. John Maynard Keynes in 1944 was invited to the Bretton Woods Convention, a multinational convention held between England and the US and other countries to discuss how to prevent nationalism that would cause another world war through a global world market. 

Keynes was was asked to help construct the world bank and the IMF. Countries also agreed structured their economies to promote labor unions, a massive welfare state, and government jobs competing in the private sector. Now this system wasn't perfect, it was essentially an economic pact with "Western" (or the "global North, or First World) countries to simultaneously combat the "Eastern" (Soviet Bloc, Second World) countries, and also exploit the post colonial, third world, "global south." However the system was a step towards further reforms in the future due to it's ideological basis in humanitarian efforts and to prevent future conflict. 

During the 70s and 80s however, economists in the Chicago school of thought, like Milton Friedman, and refugees from socialist nations like Ayn Rand, would try to counteract this new form of liberalism with libertarianism. Many present day libertarians also call themselves "classical liberals" because they want to go back to a time where the market was unregulated, but unlike the enlightenment philosophers these liberals don't view their ideology or societal structure to be a utopia, but they welcome the problems they cause. 

While a Progressive Liberal like Keynes or Mill might want to tweak the problems such as poverty and corruption that occur in a Liberal Capitalist Democracy, an Objectivist Liberal like Milton Friedman and Ayn Rand justify these problems with social darwinism. Nixon ended the US practice of control capitalism and the Bretton Woods system, and Reagan introduced the neoliberalism which was essentially the Objectivist Liberals response to Keynesian economics.

author: @StarlightPrism
text:
Great vid! While some people have good intentions, I feel like many of the people who say "classism" or "no ethical consumption under capitalism" in response to critiques against fast fashion are just doing it to brush off the issue and justify their own overconsumption, rather than making a legitimate defense of low income buyers.

I especially agree with your point about the rat race. Something that bothers me in a lot of "criticizing this is classist" arguments is that they ignore that rat race aspect. Companies don't just respond to demand, they CREATE demand. Prior to fast fashion, it was rare to have a large wardrobe. It wasn't expected (unless I guess you were a rich socialite or something) and it certainly wasn't seen as a necessity. But make fashion super cheap, everyone can buy a big wardrobe, and before long it becomes the expectation. They say that arguing against fast fashion is damaging to poor people who can't afford anything else, but most fast fashion purchases aren't done by people who are short on clothes.

Something else I want to bring up... Many people, even those concerned about ethics and sustainability, are really resistant to the idea that anyone (with exception to the ultra rich) have to give up anything substantial in pursuit of a more sustainable and ethical world. Reusable grocery bags and water bottles are easy to sell people on since no one is really attached to the disposable kind. But tell people that they need to give up, or even just cut down on, something they legitimately enjoy, it's a hard sell for most.

author: @hollynotholy
text:
This reducionism that happens so often in Twitter is the reason why I have seen, in the past year, many, MANY lies being spread like wild fire. People will see a situation, oversimplify it to the point it fits a single tweet as reply to another tweet asking "what happened??" and people will take it as absolute truth, no questions asked, no research made, no critical thinking needed.

I love watching lengthy videos on YouTube because they allow the person exposing their point more time and space for nuanced conversation, yet there are still people trying to sum up what a 50 minute video says in a 300 character comment. It's pointless; at best, it's a naïve conclusion and, at worst, it's a really malicious practice. Watching the beginning of the video with the theatrical representation of those kids argumentation just brought back so many bad memories from Twitter drama, istg.

Like many people pointed out in the comments below, people with less financial power usually try to buy things that will last and that don't cost as much precisely because they can't afford to be buying a new set of 5 different blouses every 4 months. So these people arguing this are also fundamentally misunderstanding said poor people's buying habits. There's much more nuance and paradoxes involved in poor people's buying habits than these people are willing to examine.

You'll see loads of people who work shitty, low-paying jobs with nice smartphones in their hand in public transportation even though we all live in a city known to have daily cases of people being mugged everywhere. But they need the phone to last as many years as it possibly can, so they save up a lot, pay in many installments, and also pay a fee to have phone insurance. Then they spend the next 8 years using the same phone, and if they get mugged, they get to buy a new one at a much affordable price if not entirely covered by the insurance they have been paying.

This is not even getting into the subject of rural people's consuming habits who, in many cases, don't even have access to fast fashion (or have a very limited set of fast fashion shops to buy from).

Not even joking, the city my mom was born in is huge (not rural at all; it is the State's capital, actually, so imagine rural areas there), but up until some 6 years ago had only 3 shopping malls in it. It changed after the 2016 Olympics, but my whole childhood the airport was the same and the amount of shopping malls stayed the same, too. And I'd go there every summer from the time I was 6 months old up until 2016 (so, some 19 years of my life). So smaller cities may not even HAVE shopping malls.

You could talk forever about this topic, so it's infuriating to see it being boiled down to "being against fast fashion is classist".

author: @LadyDanielle02
text:
I think you really hit the nail on the head. 'Need' is the key concept here. You need to eat, you need to have a place to live, you need to get to work and you need some basic clothing. But people don't need to participate in trends. It's maybe nice for them if they can, but it's not a life or death thing. 

I absolutely agree that we can't consume our way out of this. I feel like the best way to get ourselves out of this is to consume less...a lot less, and that's something everyone can participate in, regardless of income. Most of us don't really need any new clothes on a regular basis. Sure, it's nice to treat ourselves sometimes, but do we really need to do that every month even? Nope. And when you really look at fashion and how fast trends are cycling, it becomes pretty clear that trends are virtually meaningless anyway. Is something you have 'out'? Don't worry...it will be 'in' again in a couple of years. Seriously...

Just an aside, but I disagreed with that quote about cars being necessities in North America and Europe. Most of North America, probably (I grew up in Canada and don't think it would be easy to go car-free in most of the country), but I haven't owned a car for the entire 16.5 years I've lived in Germany and I don't feel like I'm missing anything. Oddly, even here in Berlin, a city with one of the best public transit systems in the world, people claim that you 'need' a car and that people who claim you don't are just elitist and out of touch. I don't get the 'elitist' thing at all...my transportation costs per year fall within the triple digits (including long-distance train rides). Show me a car that costs that little to purchase and run. As for out of touch, you're never further away from 500 metres from a public transport station or stop, anywhere in the city....it's designed that way. text:
Dismissal of any criticism of fast fashion as being classist also strikes me as a defense mechanism to a perceived (and probably often actual) personal attack, which I find incredibly sad because it seems like both people are on the same team. If we--as a society--collectively stopped valuing fast fashion, changing styles and overconsumption, then poor people in the Global North wouldn't feel the need to participate in such an exploitative industry. 

I think the comparison with the need to own a car is a really interesting one and potentially valuable to explore. Many people (especially in the United States) do legitimately need a car to get to work, school, groceries etc. This is a very tangible, physical problem and the solutions to it are also very real and tangible (better public transit, changes in zoning laws etc.) Fashion is almost the opposite in that the entire demand for it comes from societal values. I can sympathize with the people who feel the need to buy lots of clothes for social acceptance. wE LivE iN A sOciEtY, and societal problems can be very real to people. I think that the critical difference however is that as members of society we have a much more direct way to impact these issues than we do with say, urban planning. 

I won't claim to have the answer on how we should discuss this complex issue but I think that ultimately changing the collective consciousness of how we interact with our clothing and shopping habits is the only solution. And that will require engaging in the topic of how damaging fashion (fast or otherwise) is in a compassionate way that acknowledges current pressures while attempting to change them as well.

author: @Jasmine-gv3uj
text: I feel like what some people miss is that many low-income people have a desire (like anyone else) to wear clothes that are "trendy," which often translates to "new" (i.e. currently in style). This is what leads people to over-consume. Many brands continuously put out new products so people can buy clothes on a regular basis and feel as though they are "keeping up." If you are low-income, this shopping process is going to be limited by budget so you'd get clothes from H&M, Shein, etc. But people who are wealthier follow this same process of overconsumption, just with brands that are seen as "more sustainable" than the retail giants like Zara et al. Examples include Parade, Reformation, and countless others — all of which follow sustainable practices to a degree yet also continue the problematic process of constantly releasing and advertising new products. The problem is capitalism, and the ways in which this system brainwashes people to feel as though they never have enough and that they must constantly "keep up." Whether you're taking regular trips to H&M or Dover Street Market, it doesn't matter. People have to learn to see clothing as objects that have intrinsic value aside from how they do or do not fit into contemporary trends. In order to do this, we have to actively disinvest from capitalism and learn our own personal style, so we can approach fashion as it should be... a creative way to express ourselves and have fun with aesthetics. This is about reclaiming fashion on an individual level and ridding ourselves of the voice in our head that tells us to "keep up" and always want more. This is how we can have a healthy and fun relationship to clothes, instead of fueling insecurities that derive from capitalism and harming the environment.

author: @jlbeeen
text:
I think fashion in general can be classist. Because I remember in high school being judged for wearing older clothes, even though I did buy some fast fashion stuff to fit in. I wear a lot of thrifted stuff now, and things that I got on clearance, or still fit into from high school. I also make a lot of things myself, and a lot of my tech is older too. 
I've made clothes for really cheap from thrifted sheets, so cost isn't always the same, but it's hard to manage. Also, a lot of things that people in the USA consider "cheap fast fashion," were even too expensive for people I know (probably due to the Canadian dollar), but the people who struggled would buy fewer items, and only ones they know they would wear, as well as wearing hand me downs, and secondhand items. Yeah it wouldn't be as fashionable to wear a big 90s sweater with 2010 skinny jeans, but if that's what you have, make it work. I don't fit into a lot of fast fashion due to my body proportions, so I'm very glad I can sew and make things that work, but I'm trying to be more mindful of where I get my fabric, and how I use it. And when I do buy stuff, I look at reviews, often reviews of the exact same style that are more than a year old (mostly with footwear and underwear, shoutout to TomboyX for making underwear that lasts for a few years), and when I do buy stuff directly from China, it's because it's something I can't make myself, or can't find anywhere else. Like I have chronic illnesses, so I bought some compression socks that have zippers because that's something that makes it easier to function in my day to day life, and I got a Chinese smartwatch to help me monitor my wonky heart rate, and remind me of things. At least the watch was by a subsidiary of a company who is trying to help, by using paper packaging and making products that last (same reason why I got a Nokia phone). 
Because it's not just fashion, but other things that are seen as trends, like you mentioned TVs and cars. A lot of waste comes from fast release cycles of tech too, and where my two interests are sewing and software development, I'm pretty close to both. I acknowledge that my generational wealth has allowed me to buy more expensive things that last longer, but that doesn't mean that we should ignore the issue because not everyone has that. I do what I can by giving clothes to friends or people I know could use them rather than Value Village, and I do try to buy or make things that last, rather than things that only last a season or a year. The next step for me is trying to find a more timeless style that works for me so I can have a wardrobe that won't be too affected by trends or what others say about me.

author: @Caroline-hw9yw
text:
In general I think consuming fast fashion is immoral, but some people don't have the option to be moral. People don't acknowledge moral luck enough (the idea that some people are born into different situations that inhibit them from living as morally). We all know the classic stealing bread thought experiment, that's a perfect example. Stealing can be morally wrong but we can also understand that the person stealing bread wouldn't choose to steal if they already had bread to feed their family. And it's not really fair to compare the morality of the thief to someone who is wealthy, because the wealthy person would never have to confront the same moral dilemma.

So consumption of fast fashion, even out of necessity, is still a technically immoral action but it's not fair for people who don't need to shop fast fashion to critique the moral decisions of those who do (unless we're specifically talking about reckless over-consumption and not just material needs). Just like eating meat is wrong, but not everyone is in a position to change their lifestyle. We can make our arguments for why we should reduce consumption in all areas, but we also have to acknowledge that not everyone is equally able to abide by these ideal standards. With that being said, there is no one right argument for every case of fast fashion consumption and there is so much nuance to every case. I am still aggressively anti-fast fashion and I think people are too comfortable disregarding the insane amount of human rights violations and serious negative consequences of supporting fast fashion.

text:
thank you for actually giving nuance to how poverty is differently viewed! low income people from the global north feel compelled to participate in fashion trends while their global south counterparts are the abysmally waged workers who made their fashion forward pieces.

the debate was always weird to me, as a person from the global south, because i felt like their talking points were so simplified, and, quite frankly, reeking with privilege. on one side you say "shop sustainably" but it's upper middle class citizens of the global north hoarding and emptying thrift shops. because it's sustainable. on the other side, it's woke marxist 16 year olds saying "there's no ethical consumption under capitalism" after they either defend a tiktok zara haul or did a haul themselves. because there's nothing they can do about something as big as the culture of capitalism they are "forced" to participate.

what i always thought was the solution was if we collectively decided to change fashion culture, something that I think the mina le video talked about. sure, part of the reason is how corporate overlords have convinced us that to be unfashionable is a sin then changing what being fashionable is on a weekly basis. but if we are socially conscious enough as consumers to have a debate about it with both sides having merits of some sorts, surely we can also identify the fact that we are being manipulated into participating at all? like i said in the examples, both sides use the arguments they champion as an excuse to overconsume, whether it's thrift shops or fast fashion brands. maybe the subject of heat shouldn't be just about where you shop, but also how often, and... why? do you shop for the trend, as in you have no lack of clothing in your closet but you still regularly shop, use, and discard? questions like that.

and to be clear, I am not at all suggesting people stop trying to look good or be fashionable, because I absolutely feel that as well. maybe, small suggestion, stop or decrease dependence on being dictated what to wear? go for to aesthetics of your personal taste (i think mina le also mentioned this), or just wear what you want regardless if it's deemed fashionable today.

author: @EM-iy2nk
text: I'm from a white upper middle class family. My parents saved every dime they could despite us having a very good and sustainable income. The cycle of clothing went from first we went through hand me downs from our older cousins and what we still didn't have after going through that we were allowed to go out and buy at the mall. If we grew out of decent clothing we gave it to our younger cousins. We would wear the new and used clothing as every day clothes until they became "barn clothes" that I would wear to clean the horses stalls and ride in. Once they were too beat up to wear outside they became chores clothes for cleaning. When finally they were falling to peices they were cut into rags. We went to the mall at the beginning of summer and the beginning of the school year to fill in the gaps of our wardrobe. I thought all families did this. My parents are fairly wealthy and I'm not sure why other people don't utilize their clothes like this. My parents aren't particularly environmentally conscious or anything either. My husband grew up fairly poor and his family did the same thing. We still use our clothes this way to this day despite us both having pretty decent incomes. We also go out of our way to buy clothing used or go through what friends are getting rid of. Almost all of my riding clothes are used and I purchased them that way. I just don't see the point in buying brand new clothing and contributing to this industry.

author: @_Odyssia_
text:
As some who is in a country that is part of the "global south", but studied fashion design, this was a interesting, enlightening and telling video. It wasn't the first time I see this time a video like this, but it brought up some great points I never thought of.

I also find it interesting that the fast fashion epidemic is completely different in South Africa than it is in the "global north". Most people buy their fast fashion clothes from local stores and little boutiques that source these cheap brands like Shein, that are owned by local or foreign people. Other international fast fashion brands like Zara, H&M and Forever 21 are actually a lot more expensive to buy than that at the local clothing stores, and they aren't at every mall. Only malls where people can spend a lot cash and leisure time. However, with the rise of the internet and globalization in fashion, it has become easier to for the youth to buy online from these brands. Although, the gap isn't as large as it is the USA and Europe, and most people still prefer to buy at physical stores, there has been a rise in online shopping since 2015 or 2016. However, we do not buy so many of the same products or "mall haul" as I like to say, because it is actually wasteful. Most children and teens wear school uniforms when attending school and only need to buy clothes during the school breaks, and also limits the amount of clothes you can buy a year. Also, it's a seen as a disgusting habit to throw away your clothes if you have excess, so we universally practice giving them away to orphanages or children and people who don't have enough clothes. We are currently dealing with the effects of climate crisis from all the pollutants coming from factories and industries from the "global north", and we don't enough land for land fills, so we are urged to consume clothing products sustainability. We are urged to buy from thrift stores, wear hand-me-down clothes from our parents, and if you have the skills to sew, sew your own clothes and support local businesses, instead of adding to the fast fashion epidemic.

author: @KateRafter
text:
I'll try to keep this short. The sweatshop and fast fashion industry has made a concerted effort to brainwash American consumers into thinking cheap clothing is a right. As kind of a fashion and costume history hobbyist, I have come to understand that clothing simply MUST BE EXPENSIVE. It cannot be cheap.... unless we cut labor costs far, far below what is reasonable. The only way to make clothing cheap is through unforgivable exploitation. There is no way around this equation. Labor is the greatest consideration of clothing manufacturing. No one has yet invented a robot that can sew a garment (besides a couple of tech firms are still tinkering with mass-producing t-shirt machines). Skilled human hands are required.

For most of Western history, clothing has been expensive! I found a blog post that references what a servant in Holland in the 15th and 16th century would pay for a shirt: between 3 and 10 days of work. In today's money that starts at no less than $320 and I'll let you imagine the rest.

In 1927, a very simple everyday dress cost $5-10. That's $80-160 in 2021. And no, it's not the textiles and materials. A yard of cotton fabric for $0.15/yard then would be $2.40/yard today. Fabric has increased relatively in cost, but not too much. But everyday garments have become shockingly less expensive. Today it is cheaper to buy a garment than to sew a similar one from scratch at home, not even accounting for equipment, and that makes no sense and should scare you.

In 1960, Americans spent over 10% of their income on 25 garments a year. Today, Americans spend under 3.5% of their income on clothing and shoes and somehow get close to 70 garments per year.

So, forgive me, but the only way to right this wrong is to Make Clothing Expensive Again. Of course towards fair labor compensation, not luxury markups.

author: @camipco
text: "No ethical consumption under capitalism" seems to mean two completely different things, or rather inspire two different conclusions. One is "don't think that you can fix capitalism by buying stuff" - rejecting ethical consumerism as a complete solution to the problems of capitalism anda  replacement for structural activism. The other is "fuckit, buy whatever you want".  And this comes back to my least favorite leftist idea - that marginal improvements in oppressed people's lives are counter-revolutionary because they make people complacent / comfortable. This is the idea that condemns the centrists who legislate minimum wages or welfare improvements while maintaining capitalist structures as doing more harm than good. It sucks. Make people's lives better if you can.

text: Tbh I'm in a pretty unique position in this debate, because I'm poor, and I work at a fast fashion retail store, but I go to a private school which is mostly populated by upper middle class students. I think while it's great to update your wardrobe once in a while a lot of poor people wear hand me downs and a small collection of clothes they already cycle through, like a capsule wardrobe. Upper class kids however, it's a different story. I go to an all girls school specifically, and whether someone is part of the current fashion trends, has their own style or is part of an alternative subculture, they are always updating their wardrobe. No one wants to be seen wearing the same outfit twice. And while plenty of students have a few wardrobe pieces they really really love and do they rewear it quite a few times, they will still be updating plenty of other things to show off to friends or because it looked cool. And to be honest I don't think there's as many poor kids/people as these socialist gals think there are that even care about keeping up with trends, I've seen both in the city and my rural community that people litterally wear whatever the hell they want, a lot of the outfits don't look pretty but I don't think they really care.

text: Anyone feeling uncomfy about the video - please watch the whole video. Coming from low-income situations myself, and as someone whose dopamine gets a hit from pretty outfits, here's what I do: I still have clothes bought from fast fashion stores 10+ years ago, and a few items from less time than - I will keep and wear them for a long time. Charity shops in the UK (other than in London) seem to be a lot cheaper than thrift stores in the US, and I get plenty of pieces from there. text: I watch a lot of these videos and there's often a discussion of 'buying dozens or hundreds of pieces of clothing every year.' I figured, maybe some people do do that, or maybe it's a harmless exaggeration to get the point across. But now I'm wondering if it's not mischaracterising the situation. Maybe Zara occupies a different price bracket elsewhere, but where I live, only upper middle class people shop there. The only Zara in my state is in a very wealthy neighbourhood. Working class and poor people shop at Kmart, and usually try to get stuff on sale. I do a lot of op shopping (thrifting) now, but I only have the time bc I'm currently unemployed. The sizes can be very limited, the shops are often inaccessible for wheelchair users, if you struggle with body image it can be very triggering to be constantly trying on things and finding them to be too small, and if you have a chronic illness or disability you don't want to waste your energy going somewhere if you don't think you'll find what you're looking for. I know some people will think I'm making stupid excuses but I have several friends who want to buy more stuff second hand but don't have the time, energy or access. I totally agree with everything you're saying, and I think the people in that TikTok comments section were misusing the argument. However, this lavish overconsumption, hyper-fast trend cycles and wear-it-once attitude is not something I see a lot of in the working class. Maybe it's more of a middle class thing, I don't know.
