author: @nadinesnyder3926
text: On a personal level I know I buy clothing because my appearance is something I can control. We can't control the pandemic. We can't control horrible events we hear on the news or even what our leaders do (I live in the US so obviously we as a collective do have more control here, but as an individual your opinion does not matter) but we can control how we look. So the more cynical I feel about the world, the more into fashion I become, knowing it's an escape from facing the pain of existence.  Growing up we are constantly given the message that your appearance is what matters. That owning things will make you happy and envied. I know that this is bs but it is so much easier to give into it and buy clothing and makeup and play the game and be accepted by society. Instagram and tiktok have made this worse those apps value appearances over all else. We (in the global north) need to completely change what we value as a society. All of us (middle/upper classes) could own a suitcase of clothing and live in smaller homes that use less land and resources and still be healthy and happy.  Most people though do not have the energy to deviate from the norm. We are all tired and feel our lives our meaningless so we fill them with material objects. I don't have a solution to this. I just know that we must start devaluing objects and valuing intrinsic things as a collective, as other comments have said, because not enough people have the courage or time or energy or means to make individual actions that defy societal expectations. Honestly this is a place influencers could be very helpful. If Addison Rae or the Kardashians said hey, all the clothing I own can fit in this suitcase, I'm moving into a smaller home, and have decided to stop purchasing things I don't need and seek joy from experiences and relationships, it might help shift culture a little. Of course they make a living making us feel like shit so they can promote shit we do not need, so that will never happen.

author: @Peasant_of_Pontus
text:
Buying fast fashion does not necessitate overconsumption. Yes the business model of those corporations does rely on oversupply and giant wastage, but they drove cheap sustainable clothing options that existed prior to extinction. I'm poor living in a country that's in the global north, but not really (E. Europe). My two options are buying fast fashion made in the global south that looks okay or buy horrible looking clothes from independent market stall vendors which are likewise made in the global south sweatshops. Most of my clothes are a few years old, including T-shirts and underwear. I spend less than $100 yearly on clothing unless I have to make a big purchase (winter jacket, new shoes). I'd like to buy clothes made locally or sustainably, but they don't exist in my price range. I don't go out and buy 8 t-shirts every month to keep up with the latest trends, yet I rely on fast fashion for basic necessity clothing.

I think the onus is on the lawmakers to force corporations to create affordable alternatives not based on exploitation, but I'm scared that as always the cost of such legislation will be born by the customers while the corporations won't see a dent in their profits.

author: @SecretTwilightGirl
text:
Sometimes I hate the classist argument because as someone who grew up poor and forced to shop fast fashion because my mom could only afford clothing us through layaway or department store credit cards it's not a free pass. I'm not gonna speak for all low-income folks but when you don't know whether there'll be another back to school sale as good as this one or if you'll be able to buy anything even if it is you make clothes LAST. My mom takes such good care of the clothes some of her wardrobe is around 15 years old. And this is basic Old Navy or JC Penny brands. We weren't just buying clothes to buy. We usually waited for really big holiday sales that only happened a couple times per year. We usually only shopped for things we "needed" that had worn down like shoes that somehow always eroded on me by the end of the school year or jeans I'd grown out of. We also rarely, if ever, purged our closets just for our shopping trips. At the end of high school, most of my wardrobe was made up of clothes accumulated since elementary school. I've changed completely fashion-wise and thrift mostly but this still lingers with sleepwear. The last time I bought a "new" pajama set was three years ago. Everything else I've had since I was a teen.

I'm glad people are trying not to scapegoat us but overconsumption is something everyone can indulge in. Overconsumption and the ethicality of fast fashion have overlap but they're not always a zero-sum thing. By virtue of being poor a lot of us already do "eco-friendly" methods out of sheer necessity. Even with plastic bags, yes, plastic is never good but my family would re-use them until they literally tore apart. Or memes about POC parents constantly using random old butter containers (we were partial to keeping the plastic containers from cold cuts) for leftovers. There's definitely a choice being made in having Shein hauls every 3 months. We can definitely get into how poor people (anyone really but especially low-income folks) often have scarcity mindsets that influence their spending and consumption but that's another tangent. Overall, poor ppl aren't some Internet argument gotcha you can use or should white knight for. We're all trying to make the best of an unjust, complexly cruel world. These conversations should have more nuance and far less moral T-posing. None of us should be into social justice to feed a morality complex, it defeats the whole purpose of what we're even working towards.

text:
16:54 is amusing as someone from a third world country, cutely nicknamed "the global south"🤣but I digress.
It used to be that majority of the "waste clothes" ended up in third world countries as second hand clothes thanks to thrift shops and the US assistance that it needed to balance trade with the third world. Poor people then gained the habit of purchasing clothes with enthusiastic consumerism. I mean c'mon a dress costs the same as a pinpop. I can be as trendy as I want.

Yeaaa...no. It means local textile industries died. If that was your skill (vocation as churches train them to be) you had only the chance to work in fast fashion industry under death defying conditions to put food on the table. 
Thrifters and donaters thank you for rigorous participation in fast fashion. No honey, you were not being good by helping those poor people in Africa and Asia. It's the thought that counts, right?

And then China happened.

US has a population of just north of 340 million or there about. China multiplies that to get over billion. If US killed dressmaking China made sure it was dead for good. It shipped tons and tons of "waste clothes" to these countries. If that was not enough it corrupted the textiles that were used for local dressmaking. This destroyed the last allure of getting your dress tailormade which was the quality you got. Yey, more people in the mass clothing supply chain.

Of course that moved everyone over to second hand clothes largely from China or "original clothes" imported from...you guessed it...China. The "original clothes" are actually fast fashion only that of course what is cheap in the first world is not cheap in the third world (currency, inflation, exchange, disposable income and all that good stuff).

So how do we stop this....😉

author: @guitarlover1204
text:
One thing I am struggling to make sense of —even as a person from the global south who has direct contact with places affected by fast fashion— is this dismissal of "the right to dress fashionable".

As a socialist man it's pretty easy for me to say "don't dress fashionable if you can't afford sustainable fashion"... But I still need to dress up for a job interview; and while I might get some slack if I go there with a used t-shirt and jeans, a woman is probably not going to get the same reaction.

As far as I understand, from reading and asking female friends, not looking "good" and "put together" is a big deal for them, and while most of what this video is about is not formal clothing, that show of status and respectability through clothes doesn't stop at work. It is everywhere. 

I'm not here to say "it IS actually classist to say these things" of course not, but it is more complicated. I don't feel comfortable saying "don't buy it" because we can't stop either, and because the intersection of patriarchy would mean those women would be facing legit setbacks.

The most influential organizations in the history of humanity create these systems, expecting individuals to solve it by voting with their dollars is... Kinda strange. Not to mention that actual, legit classism can affect someone just for "seeming poor", or do I need to remind anyone of "no shirt, no shoes, no service"?

Why not advocate for actual action against these companies? Why not sabotage them, even? Why not advocate for a stop to the south's exploitation? 

This debate about fast fashion feels like it's about privileged people trying to figure out who is better than the others, instead of actually understanding and solving the issue

​@coconut_juice Kind of. While I now realize how it's maybe not the best way of putting it, as it can feel like I'm putting the social anxiety of (mostly white) women in the imperial core above, yknow, the exploitation of women in the periphery, I still think these comments skirt way too close to misogyny for me.

There are very real consequences for failing to fit within the patriarchal ideal of femininity, which is policed by society as a whole. This creates a series of needs that the fashion industry as a whole preys upon.

While fast fashion is mostly a rich people trend, as they're the ones who can afford to spend that much money on it, the reduced cost (facilitated by imperialist policies that make overseas hyperexploited workforces profitable) means  that while lower class people experience the same pressures, the more "ethical" option is a luxury they can't afford.

Expecting people to "just stop" for ethical reasons is, at least to me, a very privileged position, akin to the kind of heavy-handed PETA-style campaigns claiming anyone who isn't 100% vegan RIGHT NOW is just evil.

It's also why I say it gets dangerously close to misogyny for my liking. It's RICH people, not women, who consume the rest of us off a cliff. It's the bourgeoisie who profit from the trend, and foster the environments in which it can happen. To ignore that and just blame it on "teen girls" or whatever, is part of what makes it uncomfortable.

At the end of the day, it's a very liberal (as in the political ideology of liberalism) position, one which positions all blame at the feet of the consumer; supply and demand, individual, personal, moral choices over a more systemic view of the problem that recognizes how this is, at best, a useless demand.

That's why I qualified it as privileged people trying to figure out who is making the most moral individual decision, without actually doing anything to solve the problem.

text:
​@coconut_juice I mean, privilege does not exist in a single dimension. It's a bit of a mistake to expect to be able to count some sort of "privilege points" that you can add or subtract from people depending on their circumstances.

A poor man and a rich woman, for instance, are differently privileged. The man will not experience misogynistic oppression, while the woman will not experience economic oppression; it doesn't mean one is more privileged than the other, because privilege depends on context.

A poor person in the imperial core can indeed have a privileged perspective, and can absolutely think people should "just stop" buying fast fashion, because of it.

Some might just ignore how income limits what clothing people have access to, while people with low income might simply ignore how your appearance can limit your opportunities, specially for non-masc people.

People here in the global south (or more accurately, the imperial periphery) still have those opinions; in fact that is what drove me to make the original comment. Plenty of the women I know buy from SHEIN and similar brands as a way to get "nice clothes" that they can afford for special occasions. For a lot of people here, specially women, they represent a relatively affordable way to look "acceptable".

To deny that factor and just demand they stop for ethical reasons is kind of a big ask, specially coming from someone who wouldn't face the consequences.

This is not to say overconsumption is not a problem, it is; but it is not THE problem. It's more of a symptom of a larger system, and focusing on it is a little frustrating as someone who lives in the places they claim to be defending.

author: @ChristieBrewster
text:
A few things come to mind here, about mine and general individual clothing choices, and the reasons behind them:
• Purchasing beyond the high street is alien to me. I have a bunch of trouble with clothes I get by post without trying them on. This gives the kind of places I habitually browse from one particular thing in common. If those places were different, I'm sure that would change my habits too.
• Clothes disposability is an interesting idea, because it's a collaborative problem between retailer and consumer. My clothes from places mentioned in this video will tend to stay in my collection for years (having been bought for their visual appeal or their unique aspect that I didn't already have multiple options for.) Of course it's the fact that I have a large wardrobe that makes them last that long, if each one only had x many washes before it unravelled for good. I'm not designing a look set to match anything specifically modern, and it's not an urge I understand.
• I would like to support deserving manufacturers, but I feel like the whole world of clothing retail is out to lie and cheat and bamboozle you into believing in a saintly reputation for them. As such, there's no-one I actually trust to honestly be better than H&M (unless they're small enough that they can introduce every worker in their process). Consider the negative reputation of Nike and its factory process, when they're still not providing appreciably cheap garments by any means.
• I'm surprised this video didn't bring up what we call the 'Boots theory of socioeconomic unfairness', as exemplified in a very famous Terry Pratchett quote. It dovetails into discussing poverty and clothing choice very neatly.
• And with all this in mind, buying the more hardwearing expensive options does run into a bit of a niche where interested buyers overlap with people interested in clothes as a hobby especially their care and maintenance. Even the cheap jeans on the market could still be repaired, customised, recycled into shorts if the knees give out. But the person with those capabilities with some disposable income will be biased to pick something harder wearing, on the basis of that knowledge and appreciation.
• Lastly, women's clothing (yes, gender is a social construct, but so is clothing ourselves in the first place) have so many more options – just evidenced by square footage in any given general audience clothes store, and more than half of specialist ones. This will make gendered purchasing habits and options illuminating to compare on this topic. I'm a man, myself, and I have a feeling that doesn't come as a surprise based on how I talk about my habits. I'd love to know more about this. And about all of the above.

Legit interesting video. Would love to see a follow-up, if the response makes another crack at the topic a viable one for a video.

author: @ems9616
text:
Ok so i think what people mouthing off in this comments section need to understand is that poverty is not a competition. Poverty does not suddenly become safe or untraumatising just because others have it worse. Additionally, there is a difference between saying- 'companies like primark would still thrive even if middleclass people boycott them cause wc people have to shop there to stay clothed' and 'how dare you critisise shein hauls, dont you know its classist to see someone wasting 1000s pounds on abusively produced clothing and comment on it?' In the first case, the problem is systemic- those cheep stores are providing subsitance clothing to enough people that they can stay in buisness anyway, so a boycott would mean shaming people for subsistance. But in the second case they are clearly using hypothetical working class people as a sheild for their own wasteful behaviour.

But having said that, though i agree broadly with your conclusion, im not sure you got the balance quite right in your reporting.

To expand on this- working class people in many (not all!) Global north countries benefit from being in countries that were colonisers rather than colonised- they have good transport networks, free education, powerful banks, possibly good access to electricity, clean water, and internet. This is the source of much of the 'privalage', and lower overall rates of poverty. 

But...speaking as someone who grew up poor in england- i cant eat my internet. I grew up, like many of my UK peers; food insecure/food poor, a child carer, in a class segregated society which demonstrably does not give a fuck about our survival. And that is still traumatising, and destroys your mental and physical health. It felt at times that you were primarily approaching the impact of poverty on global northerners as... a social game. An issue of keeping up with the joneses rather than a thing that literally shortens peoples lives. In some ways, this tainted your argument about the social side of over consumption- as any wc poc person can tell you, the impacts of classist and racist descrimination from not 'looking respectable' can be severe in there own right. This isnt to defend those shein hauls- their vile and clearly only using 'class conciousness' as a way to dodge consequences for their behaviour.

 But i feel a greater emphasise on pointing that out rather than diminishing the overall argument surrounding sustainable clothing and class as a whole might have supported your argument better. As it is i cant help feeling that the video pits 'real, serious' poverty in the global south against 'social, unserious' poverty in the global north- which is deeply unhelpful and only serves to center global north middle class people as the 'virtuous savers' of the situation by chosing to prioritise sustainability over suffering. This approach is good for shein, and i will not weep when they go belly up- but its a limited perspective, because fast fashion is more than just shein, its a whole industry- and to overhaul that industry will take both indevidual AND structural changes. And to make those structural changes ethical and efective, you need to deal with (and empower!) the exploited people on both end of the chain- those living and working in dangerous conditions during production, and those living subsitance at the consumer end too. 

The people here in the comment section quibbling that somehow global north wc people should be fine, or arnt that seriously affected by poverty just because it affects us in a different way or because a different dollar number is attatched to that suffering....are being classist. As are those that dismiss the damage done by these fashion brands in the global south. But the way to resolve that is to acknowledge the multifacited and damaging nature of poverty, rather than to suggest that one type is unharmful or more frivolous than the other. And perhaps what feels frustrating about this video is not that your wrong per say... but that it feels that the end product is more interested in hashing out a theory argument between middleclass people, litigating the best way to deal with a singular moral challenge, than actually addressing the stregnths and weaknesses of boycotting as a tactic against fast fashion. 

This is in no way meant to be a hate comment, and i hope it hasnt come accross that way. But in terms of addressing the argument you set out to address, i felt this fell short. Sorry if i was incoherent or confused, i just wanted to put my thoughts accross.

author: @HumanNeighbor
text:
The thing is we also can't ask people not to enjoy their lives because they can't afford to do it sustainably. And I know this was already a pretty long video, but the bait and switch move of it's pour responsibility to consume ethically, rather than its our responsibility to create the structural changes needed to solve the problem is a big part of this. We can't boycott our way out of this, and I'm sure if you looked hard enough you'd find out so called "sustainable fashion" isn't sustainable. The trick here which was touched upon is the disposability part of our consumption. It's fine to be into fashion it isn't fine to be constantly cycling our wardrobes to keep up with the 50/year micro trends. 

Also like the misery of poverty is comparative. The visibility of economic inequality is the main problem. If I see rich people living lavish lives I feel the suffering of my own poor life more acutely. It's about the comparison. It is less miserable to be poor amongst the poor, then poor amongst the rich. You feel the unfairness of that acutely. It's why despite the fact we live in comparative luxury to the kings of old we still feel like our lives our awful, because we know how much better they could be, but have no power to actually achieve that better life. 

The main point though, is that capitalism and climate change can not be stopped by individual consumer choices. We need real institutional change,  but again we lack the power to make that change. So we're left with this weird, I must not buy nice things, because it was made with child labor choice that just leaves us miserable regardless of which choice we make. It's awful, and it's designed to be awful and paralyze our ability to act.

text: “No ethical consumption under capitalism” means it’s impossible to do NO harm. Being a moral, informed, and privileged person means doing LESS harm. The simple fact is that the shein hauls are unnecessary harm. There is no scenario where $500 shein haul is the most affordable option for necessary clothing. We shouldn’t be arguing about where to shop, instead we should be criticizing when and with what frequency do people shop. The “vote with your dollar” concept is capitalist in nature because it implies your impact is only through money. YOUR LABOR IS A MUCH MORE POWERFUL FORCE. Withhold your labor, demand your labor be compensated, if you have the ability to advocate and protect others’ labor, do that too. If you are privileged enough to by a “haul” of clothing, you are privileged enough to be educated about fast fashion, capitalism, and you have access to secondhand goods. I hate this argument because people like mommy socialist are undermining anti-capitalism and virtue signaling about classism. Wield your labor. Participate in politics and policy creation. Do as little harm as you can (buy less).

I mean, in the case of veganism, I think a more fruitful conversation would be to say, “yeah, you’re entirely correct, the way we breed and raise and slaughter animals is hella inhumane, and those of us who eat meat do participate in that inhumanity toward those animals. That is entirely fair.”

Like, animal byproducts are in glycerin, in paint, in makeup, in carpeting, in so many different things. Like, US homes built before (I think) the 1970s are built with horsehair insulation: that’s how widespread the use of animal products and byproducts are. The point is not that “oh, there’s no point!” but rather that opposing the use of animal products goes a bit farther than not eating meat and dairy.

And that’s not even getting into the issues of labor rights abuses when it comes to the humans involved in the production of food, an issue that affects more than just the meat parts of the food industry.We’re talking production plants that just straight up rent slaves from Christian drug rehab centers, and ongoing issues of migration and border-related brutality.

So yeah. Go vegan. Encourage others to do the same. But also, the main onus can’t be on the average consumer, even in the global north, to end food-industry-related cruelty.

less than 4 mins into the video but I want to add my two cents. Keep in mind that I am a black woman so I can only speak to the global majority and not the #FFFFFF perspective. 

It's an intersection of classism and racism and elitism to tell someone who is BIPOC that they shouldn't buy fast fashion. BIPOC people are generally the people who are dealing with the effects of climate change, police brutality, lack of networks for career etc so the idea of not buying a $4.99 t-shirt to vote with their dollar doesn't take in to account the full scope of the problem or why one would feel so entitled to point out the costs involved in the t-shirt but not take take their oppression in society as seriously. It's a double edged sword - someone who isn't rich wanting to stretch their dollars and be seen closer as an equal in "nice things" is not the same thing as the people who do $1000+ hauls. Its like people pointing out all the plastic waste involved in pre chopping up vegetables when people with disabilities would prefer the option and don't want to be shamed for it because they aren't the ones responsible for overproduction of plastic.

Don't spend so much time on the screen be more active .... again it's one thing if you are talking about one person but when you start pointing fingers at a large group of people doing the same thing it's probably systematic.

author: @colonelweird
text:
Say, does your researcher Nick have a famous anarchist grandpa by any chance?

Great video -- I agree with every word -- but I was waiting for that one word at the end: revolution. I feel like its absence in these discussions is the primary factor that distorts understanding. Broey's interlocutors at the beginning were borrowing leftist language to excuse their consumerism. Surely they were able to do this because leftist language has been widely used by liberals for non-leftist purposes. But the horizon of our discourse should always be revolution: the system must be destroyed, the powerless must seize power, etc. Broey used the word only at the very end, said nothing more about it, so it's not really clear what she means by it. Is revolution going to come because consumers change their buying habits? No. We should still do what we can when we make purchases, but we should not have any illusion that that will lead to revolution. We need to think a lot more about what actually will lead to revolution.

I guess this is my way of saying: Broey, please do a video on revolution and its meaning for us living in wealthy countries with moribund leftist cultures.

author: @cenobiten
text:
I really like the conclusion that you came to at the end of the video, as someone who was sucked into "radical" online spaces between the ages of around 17-21, I definitely have some familiarity with the frustration you feel. While I agree that just the tiny character limit of tiktok comments or twitter posts fails to foster meaningful analytical discourse, I think the main issues with online culture (and the for profit organisations that host them) are deeper than that...
I feel there is an appetite for ideological opposition to neoliberal capitalism, which I consider to be a good thing. However this appetite is being met through platforms such as twitter and tiktok that see stimulation (intellectual, analytical, or otherwise) as a highly competitive free market. Their apparatus encourages creators to churn out loud attention grabbing content, Just like the micro trend driven fast fashion industry encourages garment workers and designers to put out attention grabbing collections every fortnight.
To me, radical online discourse mirrors fast fashion in this way; content consumers are encouraged to engage with new ideologies so long as it is fun and exciting, and creates a niche that the market can cater to, until no more pleasure can be squeezed out of it, and a slightly different ideology gains traction. And what results is members of these online spaces not actually interested in social critique or achieving some sort of revolution but a group clinging to the power it fought for in the marketplace of ideas.

Commodity fetishm of fast fashion can lead to a momentary escape from the meaninglessness of life under late capitalism. Being radical online can feel like this too; the pure bliss of dunking on someone 5-15 years your senior in a tik tok comment section is more enticing than any advertising could be. But ultimately it's just promoting the longevity of your niche internet ideology, and acting as a sedative to the meaninglessness of postmodern living.
The term “revolutionary procrastion” springs to mind when describing genuinely well meaning radical teens, who lace their drags with jargon invented by boring German guys from the 1870s and the veneer of radicalism, without actually challenging the status quo.

What I'm trying to say may be too big and sprawling to fit in a youtube comment and all of this comes from a former radical online teen myself. A lot of this frustration I'm expressing is also directed at my former self. The remedy that I am suggesting is not that teens get any less radical, it is that their movements become less tainted by the demands of the platforms their culture exists on.

text: The cognitive dissonance I get from at the same time reading about historical dress and modern fashion industry. Following their guidance is what got us here in the first place.

author: @FelisImpurrator
text:
@JebeckyGranjola What? That makes no sense. The point is that effort put toward performative virtue by way of individual action is effectively waste energy - effort thrown into the abyss, that actually helps the capitalist power structure by distracting people with feel-good messages about protecting the environment by just turning your lights off and recycling more. By and large, multinationals operate a seller's market built on manufactured consent, captive markets, and a host of middlemen all scrambling to magically inflate "value" by paradoxically making it harder for goods to arrive where they're needed.

I said nothing about seeking to perpetuate the system, but rather devoting all of one's meaningful effort to overthrowing it if one wishes to make any sort of difference in the matter beyond feeling righteous. There are material ways in which force can be more effectively leveraged to undermine the power of capital. Changing one's consumption habits to adhere to a sort of self-flagellating personal inconvenience will never be one of those methods. It renders lettism more unappealing to the average person and one's individual ability to resist weaker due to lacking resources.

I'm a moral anti-realist, and only a moral pragmatist at most. I emphatically don't care for empty moral condemnation - that's the point. It just so happens that more ethical modes of production are more sustainable and thus more efficient for our collective survival in the long term; that's the only calculation that needs to be done to form prescriptive positions. Capitalism is indeed contradictory. It's a system built on addiction all the way up to the top, and on hyperreal pretenses, symbols detached from meaning. It creates its own inefficiency and scarcity to give itself a reason to exist.

I want my economic systems to be useful and practical and real; if that happens to be moral it's a fortunate accident. Which does seem to be the case.

author: @songbirdlyricz
text:
I get BIG triggered by this debate. I’m someone who has always had solid financial security and have been living in global north countries my whole life. I’m hyper sensitive to the issues of sustainability and workers rights and the liberation of those in the global south. At the same time, anxiety around these issues (in my personal case) is debilitating, paralyzing, and self-destructive. So the argument of “you are morally wrong for buying from fast fashion” is very difficult to navigate because, for me, it usually ends up in severe panic and paralysis. (Not super productive in changing the tides of the climate crisis or working for liberation..) 

My first instinct after hearing the back and forth in those tiktok comments is “I want to hear directly from those “poor people who can’t afford clothes” and those “exploited factory workers in the global south” that these tiktok users (who seem to not be from either of these groups) are so feverishly discussing.” Like, what do people from these groups experience? What would they say would ACTUALLY help?? 

I have several big issues with these debates that even the most well-intentioned tend to dance around. 

1) I DONT believe that shame is a productive tool to catalyze change. I feel like when we hyperfixate on minute actions of individuals and label them “morally correct/incorrect,” we just end up cultivating a bunch of neurotic, hyper anxious, paralyzed, or cynical people (who often turn to anxious consumption to cope anyway..) This was touched on in the video, but I don’t think it stuck with the conclusions being made. Why not lead with solidarity instead? What I mean by that is: i think when you care for people and make these ideal practices more accessible and sharable, then people will be more likely to engage in them. I believe the vast majority of people don’t actively want to fuck over people in the global south and destroy the planet. So what’s REALLY stopping them from adopting these preferred habits? 

2) even when addressing the larger systems outside of the individual, we still tend to place the site of change on individuals. Again, this was addressed in the video, but no alternative sites for change were really provided in the end. Of course we can’t neglect the actions of individuals and how they play into and perpetuate these systems. But for the love of god, do we not have the capacity to look outside of individuals’ lives?? Many of us are neurotically pouring over our little habits with our heads down. And then we see other individuals, and neurotically pour over THEIR little habits, and constantly compare ourselves to that person. In this way, change-making gets atomized. 

Here’s a personal example of when this self-adjustment doesn’t work very well. I mostly take care of feeding only myself. With my level of function and my lifestyle, buying in bulk turns into expensive food waste. Cooking in bulk turns into expensive food waste. Making nutrient-rich, delicious food is difficult with my time and energy resources. And without cooking and with my food needs it is extremely difficult to get the nutrients I need delivered in “purely(?)” “”sustainable”” or “”ethical”” foods. What would actually help me in this case?? Having communally prepared, delicious, nutrient-rich meals that are easily accessible and affordable (much like someone in a big family cooking for the whole family, or a church pot luck, or a school cafeteria). Instead, I rely on a lot of pre-made foods to successfully feed myself. So do “easy vegan cooking hacks” or “12 tips for cheap sustainability” offer some direction? Yes. Do they solve my main barriers to incorporating these preferable habits? No. What WOULD help in my case? Communal meals, for one. Can I get there by only hyperfixating on my individual habits? Nope. 

3)What is a “necessity”? This gets really tricky when there’s so 
many conflicting messages being launched at us. I don’t think we can honestly apply a universal standard for “needs.” In this assessment of “true needs,” we tend to neglect things like “art” and “fun” and “comfort.” Some ultra-minimalist influencers might present to you a bare, furnitureless house and conclude that this is what meeting ones bare needs looks like, for example. text: I'm commenting while this idea is still fresh in my head, so, just right after the intro. I think there's nuance to buying fast fashion when you're poor. I'll use myself as an example. I'm plus-size, so I have to buy my underwear and bras new (except for three perfectly sized bras I lucked into at Goodwill are you KIDDING me), and socks I tend to buy new just because I kind of assume everyone wears their socks until they resemble swiss cheese. I can very easily remember the past few garments I bought fast fashion: a clearance sweatshirt from Walmart last month, because the weather took a nosedive and I needed something warm, and three pairs of pants from Walmart over a year and a half ago, because I needed pants for work and the thrift store was closed due to the pan.dem.ic. I do manage to thrift most of what I need, even if it takes me a while, and I think I'm classed as a largefat. I also live out in the country with the closest thrift store being a 20 minute drive. Yeah, it's convenient for me to say that me buying fast fashion for literal near-emergencies is more in gray territory, but also, I'm not showing off my fast fashion purchases for social media clout, I'm literally wearing them so I can move about the world. Everything else I've bought, from work shirts to blouses to skirts to pajamas, I've thrifted for the past three years. I've also started learning how to mend clothing so I can make my clothes last longer. It's the mindset more than anything. Am I just trying to put fabric on my body, or am I trying to get likes on TikTok? For me, it's the former. And I'm still fashionable about it too, when I have the energy for it. I buy the fabrics, cuts, and colors that I know will look good on me and if I don't find the item I'm looking for, I keep an eye out for the next time or see if a thrifting site has something. There *ARE* a lot of options out there that aren't buying a freight load of clothes from shein or aliexpress.

author: @ayanna6327
text:
This video was great. I will definitely be putting "How Europe Underdeveloped Africa" on my reading-list! I definitely agree that fast-fashion is a problem, and it's a problem that we're largely apathetic to. I remember when I was a freshman in high school, I did a project on why Walmart was an extremely unethical corporation (and still is, it was even worse back then) that exploits people in the "third world." Some of my classmates rolled their eyes. Back then, I was a lot more reactive and extremely anti-Walmart, so I understood as I probably came off preachy (I was 15, so I'm sparing myself) I definitely would have addressed the topic a lot differently now that I have 9 years worth of hindsight. 

Basically, you said everything I wanted to, and much more with a lot more tact and nuance.

As someone who is plus-sized, I have ALWAYS struggled with thrifting. I do buy fast fashion on occasion, however when I do, I always do it with the intent of buying clothes I actually like, and not just participating in some trend for a few months, and then I'll never wear it again. That's sort of how I make "peace" with it (though I def wouldn't say equate that thought to peace.)

Also, you brought up an interesting point about how those world crisis campaigns put the emphasis on the average individual and not the machine. As individuals, we are a part of the machine, but at the same time, we are essentially forced to be a part of it. If the corporations that have created this monster were actually held accountable for the crises they create, then the situation at hand would greatly increase. While we can, and should, make efforts to be ethical, those campaigns should also directly directly target the government(s) at play for failing their people.

author: @upsetstudios1819
text:
I'm currently in fashion school and I had a very striking conversation with a classmate during my first year. 

Personally I've always been aware of the horrors of the fashion industry and ever since I chose to go into it I've had the existential dread of "what if I have to join the fast fashion industry in order to work in fashion?". Choosing to be hopeful and aim for slow fashion to the best of my abilities. 

But in my first year, I met this woman, let's call her Pam. Pam was a grown woman with children who had fled Pakistan only about a year prior and came to Norway. She was now enrolled in a one year textile course and she seemed very excited. 

A few weeks in, we were talking about where we'll end up after fashion school. She was very excited to work with her hands and sew lots of garments, possibly with some pakistani influences. Hoping to give her some perspective, I decided to tell her the truth: 

Fashion graduates in Norway don't sew. We sit in offices at Bik Bok, Zara, H&M, designing clothes and sending said designs to factories in the global south. We're usually in the top few, deciding the workload for thousands of garment workers that make breadcrumbs compared to us. My teacher in a different university even designed clothes for Bik Bok for over a decade. In Oslo alone there's like 4 different fashion schools. If we decide to design indigo dresses, then thousands of liters of dye and chemicals will be dumped into the river systems in the global south. 

And I could see the same heartbreak in her as I have felt, only I can't imagine fleeing a country of war to seek a better life in the world's richest country, only to learn your true passion might lead to suffering to those who couldn't flee

author: @KalynnCoy
text:
Thank you for putting this out! I have a degree in fashion and ultimately ended up leaving the industry because it was so unsustainable and contributed to my climate anxiety to such an extent- I'm now in academia studying the effects of influencer endorsements, so this video is right up my alley. I've gotten into a lot of internet fights with people who argue that fast fashion is "good, actually". There tends to be a lot of privilege in that perspective- even from economically marginalized communities in the "global north". 

We should also emphasize how quickly fast fashion has emerged, especially sites like Cider and SheIn. Because the growth of these sites has been so, well- fast- most of the data we have if from before the emergence of these retailers. Instead a lot of the data on fast fashion figures only look at Zara and H&M versus the hyper fast fashion retailers. And although Zara and H&M are bad, they are less horrible than the online only fast fashion platforms-consequently, our understanding of the environmental and social impact of fast fashion is likely underestimated, given that these platforms are incredibly opaque about their sourcing, production, and shipping tactics. We literally do not know just how bad these firms are to the planet.

‘The reason that the rich were so rich, Vimes reasoned, was because they managed to spend less money.

Take boots, for example. He earned thirty-eight dollars a month plus allowances. A really good pair of leather boots cost fifty dollars. But an affordable pair of boots, which were sort of OK for a season or two and then leaked like hell when the cardboard gave out, cost about ten dollars. Those were the kind of boots Vimes always bought, and wore until the soles were so thin that he could tell where he was in Ankh-Morpork on a foggy night by the feel of the cobbles.

But the thing was that good boots lasted for years and years. A man who could afford fifty dollars had a pair of boots that'd still be keeping his feet dry in ten years' time, while the poor man who could only afford cheap boots would have spent a hundred dollars on boots in the same time and would still have wet feet.

This was the Captain Samuel Vimes 'Boots' theory of socioeconomic unfairness’.
-Men At Arms, Terry Pratchett

author: @BryanBMusic
text:
I definitely agree that the Global North often erases the struggles of the Global South.  

However I also struggle with when/where to discuss individual behavior, especially because at one point all of us will be throwing stones in glass houses.   For example, someone could call out your waste of resources unnecessarily to add decor to your video (excess shoeboxes, paper bags, print outs, etc).   Also most of us across class lines have more than one pair of shoes in the global north.  Where should the line be drawn?  

At the same time I definitely see people weaponize “no ethical consumption under capitalism” as a pass to be inconsiderate.  I think it’s really dicey with no clear answer. 

Overconsumption is an issue but to overly frame it as an individual choice lets the system stay in tact.  

I think we should encourage each other to do our best and also offer grace when people fall short of perfect.  And still place most of the ire at corporations and people in power.

author: @zekec6088
text: There's several classes in the US that are ubiquitously referred to as poor. There's the homeless underclass who are our untouchables, people who have to steal tampons and food and take drugs to survive and have nowhere safe to sleep.  There's the 'ducks' - barely staying afloat, overworked and underpaid people who are heavily indoctrinated with resentment towards the unhoused/houseless/homeless class for getting /anything/ they need to survive that they didn't buy, as well as often the disabled class (those who have by some miracle navigated the system and become legally sanctioned as disabled enough to receive SSDI while at the same time proving themselves abled enough to successfully jump through all the hoops and prove they meet the criteria and really need or who get something for 'free') while some members of the disabled class disdain the houseless and homeless for stealing and other crimes of survival and for self-medicating outside of legally sanctioned substances (though many legally disabled as well as ...some... working class people do feel solidarity with the untouchables ...or at least a humanizing degree  of compassion). Work for pay is becoming so soul--sucking, exhausing, and lonely that people with jobs literally envy the unhoused on the street and those unable to work due to being disabled, but still they - half the time - turn on those homeless and disabled individuals rather than the boot heel of capitalism. I've read various stats that 36 homeless folks die in the US each day and that 1,500 unhoused individuals have died in Los Angeles since the pandemic began... but both of those are low, no doubt.  There's also a divide, I think, between families with kids and single adults, cos single adults can often afford to squeak by on wages that wouldn't support another person ... it seems like parenthood has become steeply more financially detrimental in the past couple decades, and most young people literally cannot afford to have kids, while the ones who do are increasingly in greater insecurity. Then state's take away the kids of poor people to redistribute them to the middle and upper classes rather than provide them with the resources they need to support parenting. Meanwhile abortion's (-legal) becoming obsolete. The opiate rages as intensely as the pandemic and rich drug users can spend 5 or 6 digits on a rehab stint, while receiving sympathy and adoration form press and public while those with addictions who cannot afford any kind of humanizing care get nothing but disdain and treated like garbage. I hate it here.

​@taliahturqoise9673 given how quickly fast fashion changes, how clownish some trends are, and how often trends are recycled, I'm genuinely unsure how clothes from a thrift store could be identified as "dated" at this point in society. Thrift store selection depends on location, but all the ones I've been to, the clothes are generally in good shape. Their main problem is a basic lack of material needs and shelter and security; the general conditions of their clothing is simply a reflection of that damage, not the culprit. Pointing to the homeless as an example of why looking fashionable is important and why thrift stores aren't good enough is a little....tokenizing. author: @theMoporter
text:
@AshaA2 The fact is that cheaper clothes used to be of higher quality. If you're from a lower class family, and you look after your clothes, you can see the difference in items from the same shop between the decades - seams made looser, cotton T-shirts made thinner, denims less sturdy. Brands that have existed for over a century have either raised their prices or gone fast fashion.

As for the condescension over sewing, you're aware that it's a...skill? It's not easy just because we're used to it. If you have any dexterity issues or RSI, simple tasks that an able-bodied child can do, like sewing a button, are difficult or impossible. Accessibility tools exist but are an excess cost. Children assigned male are shamed for doing "girl stuff", or even barred from learning because it's "women's work". It takes time and practice before you can fix work clothes without them appearing as unprofessional. There's a bunch of cheap sewing supplies, but anyone who's used them knows the pins, needles and scissors dull quickly and the thread is awful. Basic knowledge, like what material the thread should be, requires going out of your way to learn. If you need to know more than that, you'll have to collate a lot of often contradictory sources.

I was taught basic sewing techniques by my mother, given many (cheap but decent) supplies to practice on, and had the mental and physical ability to easily learn. Even though I was taught because we had to be thrifty, if I didn't have a knowledgeable parent with time and money enough to teach me, or if I'd been incapable of threading a needle, then I wouldn't have had those opportunities. Just because YouTube tutorials exist *now* doesn't mean there aren't multiple barriers to entry. You can't reasonably expect all poor people to have skill and equipment (or the resources to gain them) to be able to work on their own clothes, any more than we can all work on our own cars.

If the lack of dressmaking ability in the working class is offensive to you, volunteer to teach a class at your community centre. It isn't the problem hetr.

text:
When I was a broke student, as terrible as it sounds, I didn't feel too torn up about buying stuff at H&M, because it was pretty much all I could afford if I really needed something. That 10$ sweater I bought in 2016? I wore it at least once a week, and I still have it today. Thrifting wasn't an option for me, because all I could find were granny clothes, and the only sewing machine I had access to was my mom's, which was broken and she didn't want to have it fixed, and I couldn't afford to get it fixed either, nor could I buy one, because again, I was broke. 

Not so fun story: I worked at Costco later on, on a seasonal basis, and I had another job during the school year, for the simple reason that Costco wouldn't let me work less than 25 hours a week during the semester if I became an official part-time employee, which would have led me to a burnout, guaranteed. From time to time, when I saw some clothing that was "okay" and didn't age me too much, I'd buy it, because it was relatively cheap compared to other places. I own, like, 60 pairs, lol". I waited for her to leave to go out and cry in the bathroom. Looking back at it, it feels extremely silly of me, but at the same time... who the hell needs 60 pairs of jeans?!?!?!

text:
@AN-sm3vj I like some of the points you've made. But I would like to add some caveat. 
#1. Just because an individual cannot change a system by themselves does not preclude them to live within the normal distribution of consumption if their goal is to change the system. People do have self agency to live out their virtue and change does not come without sacrifice and it starts with what most people can control, self agency. But of course, voting in America is the start of exercising real political power for an individual in the u.s.
#2. Yep, correct on our laws. We have exported all of the external cost of our consumption. This is known as nimby, and the push for sustainability is the capital system feedback mechanism for correcting the error. Sustainability is usually seen as maximizing both shareholder and stakeholder value. The prior system of capitalism only emphasized maximizing shareholder value. Now, what is a stakeholder? Good question, no one really knows. 

People are stuck between a rock and a hard place in the USA. Basically, the central bank and the government colluded to give the owning class the best opportunity to borrow money after the financial crisis. This was done with good intention, which was to create a soft landing for the economy after the housing bubble, but the ramification is what we have today, a greater accumulation of wealth at the top, shrinking middle class, and no good solution to fix the wealth gap. I don't really have any good answers to any of these issues as nuance is key, and no one have time for nuance.

Ohh and one last thing, the internet has virtually democratized the free flow of information and for many western nations, the barrier to massively assemble can be achieved globally due to the internet. It's more of a want to change that is keeping the working class to unite, as intended by the market system. This only proves or signal why capitalism is resilient, it can respond to information and make adjustment to correct for information to satisfy the market demand. It keeps people fat and happy because that maximizes shareholder value, which makes it hard to upend.

I don't understand how """poor""" people can afford to buy the new seasonal fast fashion every season...
I still wear the same jeans I wore in highschool, I still wear old Aeropostale shirts from early 2010. And don't even get me started on how old my winter coat is.

The thing is, even though many "fast fashion" clothes are made cheaply, you can make them last of you just care for them and mend them when they need it. I exclusively buy from these cheap stores, and make it LAST. 

I cannot afford even the cheap fast fashion that these """poor""" people on twitter are buying.

I wore them every day in highschool during the cold seasons, and I was bullied because "you wore that yesterday!" as if washing machines don't exist. It's easy to say "just buy less clothes if you're poor, buy some good ones and make them last" but you need to address the classist discrimination people will face for wearing the same clothes repeatedly.

author: @tyquira
text:
The thing that's so frustrating about the argument with fast fashion/poverty is that people will go out of their way to blame corporations. Like I had an argument with a friend where they were complaining about shoes and how they kept falling apart, and I gently pointed out that a store nearby had good quality shoes and the cost was only slightly more expensive (like I think $10-$30, I don't gouge shoe prices but they're not more expensive than what I see at bigger retail stores), and I had a few pairs that had lasted me several years, as opposed to other places where I'd be lucky to get 6 months wear out of them. I then added, kinda as an afterthought because this kind of stuff is important to me that it was a small business and the shoes are cruelty free. Immediately they went on the defensive like I was judging them and said "it wasn't their fault it's the corporations!" Which like, is true. But it highlights this weird disconnect we have with taking care of our planet. Like, I hate to tell you this but if climate change legislation does go through its not just going to impact the lives of people at the top, it's going to impact everyone. Society's fabric will have to change from the bottom up. Everyone will have to change their lifestyle to consume less and we will probably consume less animal products and buy less shoes. Like this will happen if taking care of our planet takes the center stage of society's conversation, whether we like it or not. The disconnect is incredible.

Edit: so clearly this comment was taken in the worst way possible where people automatically assumed that I was talking about poor people where it will break the bank if they spend one cent more than what's being asked of them, and it's their fault there's a climate crisis; I'm not having this argument with people, it will go in circles. 

My point was specifically if you're a person who can afford to choose, you should be able to choose, when MOST people I KNOW personally CAN choose to not take Ubers or not shop at fast fashion or spend a little bit more upfront to get a better quality item, and they DON'T because it's slightly more comfortable for them in the short term not to. The person I was talking to in this situation has more money than I do (I've seen her paychecks!) and could easily afford a better quality pair of boots if she wanted to; if that doesn't apply to you, fine. Most of us can be honest with ourselves on whether or not that's true and do the math.

My point was that a lot of people don't seem to understand that if the care of our planet is made the priority it should be made, then everything will change. For example, if factory farming has caps put onto it, animal product production will be much more expensive which means that a lot of us who consume animal products now may not be able to in the future. Animal products will probably be considered even more of the luxury item it is now and much more expensive. If abusive factories stop being a thing, the fast fashion aka cheap clothes will not be as readily available, meaning that better quality items will be. They seem to think that they can go on living their life as is because well, blame the coorporations, it's not our fault, our way of life is 100% sustainable but these damn coorporations, screw em. 

And it starts with people who have a choice in whether or not they will support ethically made items/ethical companies and by and large, they are not making that choice.

author: @HereIAm247
text:
As someone who have been there, it is not only about buying the big name brands - it is more about buying things with intention, and using each item until it is worn out (and trying to extend that day as much as possible). :)

I never buy the super expensive brands either, but there are plenty of brands in the middle range, who produce good quality, which costs more than fast fashion (but not nearly as much as designer brands).

Most people just buy a lot of things without an intention, and wonder why they never have any money. They can spend 500 $ on 50 items, and wonder where their money goes, and why they have a closet full of clothes, but never have anything to wear. Because the things they buy are more often impulse buys they don't really like. Therefore, they don't get a lot of value for their money. Because they spend lots of money on things they don't use.

If instead they spend the 500 $ on 12-25 items of higher quality, they would have fewer items, but all of them would get used. Think capsule wardrobes. Not that you need to get that low on items in total, but they are created/curated with intention, and can be mixed and matched with most pieces. Because the items are higher quality, they last much longer than the other wadrobe. Because everything gets used, you get great value for money. 

In the long run, investing in higher quality will save you money, because it doesn't need to be replaced as often. :) Just go for the best you can afford, and try to curate your items, and buy with intention. This limits the amount of things you end up throwing away unused (money wasted), and you love the pieces more, because they were actually bought with intention. 

So over 10 years, you may have spent 500 $ on clothes, whereas your fast fashion wardrobe would have cost you 2.000+ $ in the long run. It is about long term thinking. If you thrift shop, you probably already use this method; you buy with intention. This is the main message when people are talking about cutting out fast fashion. To buy and wear with intention, so you get value for your money. Wether or not it is a high or a low price tag. :)

text:
I remember, maybe back in 2019, that a Forever 21 store had closed in an area that I considered had overly priced clothing, and the price of their final sale items were phenomenal. My mother and grandma bought final sale pieces that were as low as $1. At the time, I regretted not spending time with them to catch that opportunity, and I remember feeling bad that Forever 21 had closed. 

After this revelation and journey that I've found out about fast fashion has now made me glad that Forever 21 did close in that area. I still have those $1 pieces that my mother handed down to me. /!\ Read this to make your school more eco friendly /!\
Please make your school organise a clothes trade. In my school we cleared a spot in the hall for people to drop their old clothes and pick 'new' ones. Then at the end of the week (we did this for climate week) we donated the leftover clothes to homeless shelters.
The clothe industry is the 2nd most polluting industry in the world and second hand and trade are an important solution. Please try to do this in your school by proposing it to your environmental club, your students' house or even asking your principal.
In my school, and especially in my section, we have a lot of ecologists and activists and we are therefore pretty aware of the issues with our environment. We organise a lot of things (#1pieceofrubbish, #FrydaysforFuture,park cleaning, trash art, gardening sessions, conferences and debates maybe a future school compost...) and still have a lot planned.

text: I lived in Manhattan in the 1970's. One of the things that blew my mind the most was that every 6 months you could see, it seemed like everyone, wearing the next greatest fashion. It is our lack of self worth, and I don't mean our ego aggrandizement, that is our problem. We think to have expensive things makes us worth something. It doesn't. It makes us stupid, ignorant and mostly out of touch with who and what we really are.

author: @korichamberlain
text:
Most clothing that is worn once isn’t actually immediately thrown away. (A US perspective) It may stick around someone’s home for a couple of years before being donated to a charity shop. If it doesn’t sell at the charity shop/thrift store it gets sold off in bulk for “recycling” (if they don’t just throw it away) and gets shipped abroad. From there it might get reused, but is more likely to end up in a landfill on another continent. 

The point is, there is a whole system in place to make it seem like clothing isn’t actually going straight into the trash. It’s the other half of the illusion that lessons the sensation of waste.

author: @StephiSensei26
text:
This program was just too short. There needs to be a follow-up program. The topic is too important to simply leave it here. Thank you DW for your fine programs of world impact.
Personal note: What we are dealing with here, in my opinion, is control of the popular mindset. We as a culture, Western Europe, America (in particular), Japan and upcoming China, are being and have been for quite a while, manipulated by the textile / fashion corporations, to believe that "we need" something, which we do not "Need". Their entire reason for existence is, simply put, to make money. Making a useful durable product and selling it, is not in their interest, because it takes too long. Faster and cheaper is better. The drug companies here in the US do exactly the same thing, only their "target demographic" may vary. It's targeted at older people instead of Teens and Youth. The minds of the young are malleable, and that's what they want to really sustain. Like the women studying to become psychologists, they have already become prey to the schemes and plots of the industry.
I don't expect we can ever go back to "the good old days", when we made at least some of our own clothing, certainly not with the Capitalist work culture we have now. "Wake, Work, Earn, Buy, Use, Discard, Eat, Sleep and Repeat!" Owning something which you made yourself, has value and pride built into it. "Cool" junk stuff on a rack, does not. (I once had a Jeans Jacket, on which I embroidered a large butterfly over the back. I wore it until it recycled itself! Fashion and Individualism built into one.) We have lost touch with what value really means. And the industry depends on this weakness of mind. Our lives are too distracted and stressed, and the "Industry" likes it that way. As long as they can keep us distracted, dizzy and entertained by the next "cool" thing, they'll stay in business, and the world will just get messier in their wake.

In this video, fashion entrepreneur Josephine Philips discusses the environmental impact of the fast fashion industry and proposes solutions to address it.

Consumer Culture: The author highlights that our current habit of buying and quickly discarding clothes is unsustainable (1:25–2:00).

Personal Stories: Josephine explains the importance of shifting our perspective on clothing through stories about her grandmother’s dress and her sister’s jeans (0:08–1:07, 3:40–4:48).
Conclusion:
In conclusion, the author urges us to view items not just as commodities but as a part of our lives, and to consciously change our consumer habits (6:50–7:45).

text:
The idea that simply keeping and repairing our clothes could contribute to solving climate change is surprisingly powerful. Josephine Philips argues that fast fashion fuels waste and environmental damage, and that valuing what we already own is part of the solution. Her point challenges the mindset of constantly buying new items just to follow trends.

I think her argument makes sense, especially considering how much textile waste ends up in landfills. At the same time, the issue feels more complex than individual choice alone. Fast fashion is supported by large companies, aggressive marketing, and affordable pricing that makes it accessible to many people. Not everyone has the option to invest in durable clothing or repair items easily.

Overall, the talk highlights an important shift in thinking, but long-term change will likely require both personal responsibility and industry-level reform.

text:

Second, you have to put in energy and resources to recycle. It isn't free. Papers needs de-inkers and bleaching agents. In some cases the total footprint of recycled resources exceeds the footprint of new resources. 

The proliferation of synthetic textiles, including mixtures of natural and synthetic textiles, is creating a recycling nightmare. Natural fibers can’t easily be separated out for eventual reuse or recycling, while polyester clothes are likely to rot in landfills for hundreds of years. text:
I won’t buy second-hand clothes anymore. I bought so many second-hand clothes on Vinted that ended up being damaged or the wrong size. I’ve decided that it will be more responsible for me to buy a small quantity of new clothes that fit me, can be returned if something is wrong, and come with a guarantee.

Buying second-hand can also be a consumerism trap. We might end up spending more and buying more just because second-hand items are usually cheaper. As a result, many of us fill our wardrobes with clothes we don’t wear because they don’t fit well, and we bought them just because they were cheap.

text:
I have so much to say on this topic. I love fashion but I have changed my approach to shopping for clothes over many years. One reason is that I saw the decline in quality and breathable fabrics in stores that I frequented/frequent. What used to excite me, like getting a cheap dress I now think is a waste of time, especially if it's fast fashion. I think about how I may have something similar in my wardrobe, or that I have a certain amount so I don't need another one. Or if it is seriously that poor quality how long would I expect it to last? I got sick of throwing clothes out. I was actually embarrassed with the amount that was coming in/going out. I'm nowhere near I'd like to be but I have improved a lot this year with my shopping habits. 
I've also really started thinking about the people that make these clothes and how they are exploited. And honestly, the more I think about who they are, what they get paid, how they live.....it makes me think that dress with the cute print is not worth it. 
But the most important reason for me is now I have a child and I think about what kind of person that I want to raise. Hopefully if I am mindful, then he will be mindful. If I consume less then hopefully he will too.

author: @kotykivna
text:
I am a Ukrainian woman. As for clothes, 7 years ago I gradually switched to clothes made by Ukrainian manufacturers. Over the past 6-10 years, literally hundreds of Ukrainian clothing brands have emerged that sew high-quality clothes - and some of them create such beauty that no Zara can compare to. However, such clothes are sometimes very expensive - much more expensive than fast fashion. Why did I switch to Ukrainian manufacturers in the first place? I saw that clothes from Zara, Massimo Dutti, H&M, Cropp, Medicine, and many other well-known in our country brands are expensive and the quality is terrible. In Ukraine, I can buy clothes made from 100% natural fabrics several times cheaper than plastic sweaters and dresses from fast fashion brands.

But the most important thing is that on August 1, 2023, I started a no-buy year, and on August 1, 2024, I extended it for another year. I donated hundreds of things, threw away a lot of them (because they were old and worn out, but still in the closet), and realized that 50 things would be enough for me to live on, and I have at least 200 more, so I definitely won't need new clothes for at least the next 5 years. Except for 2 pairs of shoes - I buy shoes very rarely, and the shoes I have now (also all made in Ukraine) have been worn for 3-4 years.

author: @EmL-kg5gn
text:
Firstly I loved this video, thank you! Secondly my venting

There’s been 2 main difficulties for me in avoiding fast fashion. One is severe chronic fatigue. I can sew and crochet and shop secondhand - if I’m well enough. I’m hardly ever well enough. The other is the combination of sudden weight changes due to medical issues and unusual proportions. Most clothes don’t fit in any size so I’m always tempted to buy anything that almost fits. I’d never had size changes as an adult so I hadn’t learnt how to handle it and I didn’t have much energy to plan well. Or time! Every weight change happened in either a few weeks or a few days. I tried to make do with clothes that didn’t fit but sometimes I truly couldn’t, public nudity is illegal and probably cold haha. And sometimes I got fed up with the physical and psychological discomfort of ill-fitting clothes and caved to fast fashion

So I now have mini-wardrobes in 5 sizes. I don’t have room to store it all and I’m unlikely to have the medical issues that caused the weight changes again so I’m living in the mess until I have energy to give away or sell the clothes (I don’t want it to go to landfill). I’d love to make adjustable clothes with some fabric I have, the designs are in my mind already but I need energy. If anyone actually reads all this and has advice I’ll take it!

author: @almalauha
text: One of the issues is trends, and how because of social media, the trend cycles have gotten shorter and shorter. I was born in the mid 1980s so was a teenager in the later 90s and early 00s. YouTube didn't exist, there was no Facebook, there was no smart phone (the mobile phones didn't even have a camera yet). Most people don't have enough money to overhaul their wardrobe every, say, 3 months with quality items made by people who are getting a fair salary. So there's a demand for very low cost trendy items that people don't expect to wear that many times, and fast fashion jumps in to supply this demand. People only want to pay a couple of £s for a trendy top, and Shein and the like will make it happen (just don't ask them how!). The problem lies with the consumer, they are the demand for this. And as the consumer we have the power to change this. I too experimented with fashion when I was a teen but then ended up mostly settling on my own style that I have had for probably around 15 years now. I've always seen it as lame to want to change your style to follow trends, to me it shows you don't have any creativity or aesthetic personality.

author: @almalauha
text: As consumers we have a lot of power. Simply do not buy services or goods from companies you disagree with. It's not up to the government to fix everything you see as an issue, it's up to you as the individual to live according to your own ethical views as much as possible/as much as you care. It is totally possible to greatly reduce how much you (have to) rely on fast fashion. Firstly, use what you already own. I have a couple of garments and several bags that I have had for 10-15 years and that are still going strong. Secondly, take good care of what you already have by washing it according to the care instructions (I think the drier damages garments a lot so airdry if you can), and by mending/fixing rips and tears etc. Thirdly, buy second-hand when you need/want something that is new to you, and sell or donate your own stuff that is still good but that you no longer need/want. Finally, you can also learn to alter, tailor, make, and even design your own garments. It's not that hard to learn the basics and a second-hand basic sewing machine is well within many people's budgets. You can then easily take in or shorten garments that you already own, add some embellishments on it to give it a new look, tailor it to fit you better so you'll enjoy it for longer etc. I am vegan because I do not want to be part of animal exploitation. I am not waiting around for the government to ban all animal agriculture, I am choosing to not be part of an industry that I disagree with. I do the same, as much as is convenient/possible, with fashion/garments. This is available to almost everyone in the west.

text: Love this video, but I do think it's important to differentiate between "fashion" as a general concept and the fashion industry. I'm Black and Indigenous and textile making and weaving were (and still are) extremely important in both cultures. You hit it on the head, though, that this idea of mass production and changing trends are 100% a result of capitalism and imperialism. In those cultures, self-expression through fashion is truly possible *because* people are making their own fabrics and items. I think in a lot of Leftist circles (and in some of the comments), the idea of "self-expression through clothing" and "aesthetic" gets way too muddled. There's nothing wrong with wanting to look nice and be comfortable--people have been doing that long before capitalism. But while trends are broadening these days, self-expression is stifled significantly through mass production and the trend cycle. So both can be true at once. That's why the idea of upcycling and reusing gives me a lot of hope; it's not only good for the workers and the planet, but good for self-expression and truly *interesting* fashion as well!

text:
just a related anecdote on the topic, my late grandmother's older sister worked as a seamstress for a small-time clothing brand in my home country. Back then, there was no ready to wear clothes, you had to come in, get measured and receive your tailor-made clothes days after. She said that when ready to wear clothes became more common, her line of work ended. I had the privilege to talk to someone who worked in one of these fast fashion sweatshops. They told me that you're not a seasoned worker until you've had accidents with the sewing machine. And true enough, the hands of this former worker showed it, scars upon scars of it. The most saddening part of it was as important as their job is, they don't get credit nor respect for it. To top it all off, this worker got laid off for being too old and too slow to work at the factory's pace. In my opinion, fast fashion is one of those hook, line and sinker tactics capitalism has devised, and the lot of us just gobble it up. We buy because the system that we work for wears us down too much, which ironically fuels the system to wear us down some more. Ever since I learned that my country had small businesses that offer good quality and custom-made goods, I have almost shunned away from fast fashion and its ilk. I can't remember when I last bought a new pair of jeans or a new shirt. I just wear the ones that I already have.
EDIT: as our changing climate said, we can't buy our way out of fast fashion, but the very least we can do is to call them out and exploit their exploitation.

author: @sabrinusglaucomys
text:
The idea isn't to blame impoverished workers, it's for everyone watching the video to join unions, support strikers, and help build an international labor movement so that better-off workers are doing their best to organize alongside those who have fewer resources and protections. Hopefully eventually our efforts can combine to yield adequate results.

Of course people need to also take consumer and voting actions when possible, but those avenues don't work well b/c there's no way every individual consumer is going to choose to overcome the power of the advertising industry telling them they need fast fashion, and voting (at least in the US) doesn't seem to offer any avenue of challenging capital (the far right has captured much of the political system via anti-democratic means and the only other available party is still just liberal capitalists). 

It's a good point that workers organizing is easier said than done given that capitalists have forced billions of people into desperation but it *doesn't* require workers to care about the environment or any of these issues in the abstract, just to care about their own survival and fighting for better wages and working conditions, so some people think it's a better use of energy to try to build worker power than to tell people to fret about their individual purchases. 

If there were a clear way to solve the issues of capitalism we'd have done it by now so it's fair to think that voting or consumer movements have a better chance than garment workers organizing, but they've certainly been tried a ton without much success--and we can see corporations/elites pushing these other solutions *because* they don't think they'll succeed.
