text:
Right, under capitalism social media is paid for by ads. So naturally it's a huge driver in creating demand for fast fashion. If social media were collectively owned and paid for, just *not having ads* would cut out a huge amount of demand for fashion. The people running it could also carefully think about other mitigating steps, like how to avoid giving more clout/visibility to people just because they look attractive in their photos, which would help not only reducing the demand for eye-catching fashion but also combat looksism and other biases, plus probably help with eating disorders and body image issues etc.

And a big part of the argument in the video is just that, even if a collective of workers producing clothing were acting to maximize profit, it *wouldn't* do so to the detriment of the health of its own workers and therefore would have to slow production down considerably compared to the current fast fashion industry. But there's no reason that we have to imagine a future where the world's still populated by roving bands of bourgeoisie looking for anything they can sacrifice in the name of profit. Just because a potential for profit exists, doesn't mean anyone will try to profit off it, and for most of human history profit was not in fact how people or groups made decisions.

author: @morethanyourbasics
text:
i am a black woman in canada in my 30s. i still fit a lot of my clothing from high school. I got a lot of hand-me-downs. I also got into thrifting as a teenager and in my early 20s. A lot of my clothing is fast fashion with some vintage items. 

I have a hard time visualizing the kind of consumer that is constantly shopping or constantly buying trends. That person is in a different category than me. My clothes last a long time because I don't want to be back in the stores replacing things and I don't see items as disposable. However shopping "sustainable" is time consuming to research and can be a gamble in terms of liking how everything fits. 

I will say that I am really good at spotting quality. I can spot the quality leather item in a thrift store just as I can find the best quality jacket in a "fast fashion" store. (in person not online). I think getting acquainted with materials is a great start for people to reign in on what is quality. I'm also now at the stage of life where I am willing to tailor more. I also find leaning into pieces that give you joy or get you the most compliments. For example I'm known for a light blue jacket that wear with many things which isn't the "beige and grey" trend but is personable to me and my personality and the fact that I'm a graphic designer/artist.

author: @mickaylastar
text: You see, people who are not anywhere close to poor will justify their consumption behavior, ie buying loads of cheaply made clothing, by saying that poor people rely on these brands to have any clothes. 1) That excuse doesn't apply to most of the people using it, and 2) people actually living near, at, or below the poverty line do not buy from these brands because they literally cannot afford to waste their dollars on items that may be unwearable upon delivery; they shop at thrift stores (now becoming too expensive for actual poor people) and Walmart (still fast fashion, but nobody is buying hundreds of $$$ in Walmart clothes because it isn't cool to shop at Walmart), where they can see the clothes in person and budget out what those clothes are worth versus the dollar cost of them. It's people who are NOT poor who can afford to potentially throw money away on items so poorly made that they might not be wearable or that have to be replaced after 1 wear. It's people who are NOT poor who think "affordability" means "I can afford to buy a lot more cheap items, and I wouldn't be able to do such large hauls if I bought clothes that aren't cheaply made." They aren't considering cost-per-wear because the intention from the outset is to buy as much as possible so they don't have to repeat outfits. The entire mindset is backwards; a generation brought up watching Disney characters brag about never re-wearing clothes and watching people on the Internet do the same has taught young people that you should think of "affordability" in terms of buying as much as you can so re-wearing doesn't have to be a consideration. "Capsule wardrobes" used to just be called "wardrobes"; now it's seen as some sort of niche high effort to buy items you know will go with other things you own so you can wear your clothes more often and buy less.

author: @DragonriderEpona
text:
Some tips from someone who knows how to sew when looking for better quality clothing:
- Look at the materials. Avoid synthetic fibres like polyester, polyacryl, nylon (basically anything that starts with poly-)  in anything that isn't meant to be  waterproof. Your skin can't breath in those and if you're like me with sensitive skin, sweating in those can cause rashes. 
Clothes with up to 5% elastane/spandex are fine. 
- Look at how thick (see-through) the fabrics are. If you can see pretty well through, you might need to check out things out first, before deciding whether it's good quality or not. Do a stretch test: How does the fabric act (about to rip?) when you pull it. With knitted garments it's always better to do a strecht test first and look how big the loops are. Usually bigger and looser loops will cause the garment to lose its form quicker.
- Look at the seams! Are there a lot of loose threads? Are there any other threads that can be pulled easily? If yes, it's not worth buying it! 

If you're interested in sustainable clothing brand, there are lists online with all kinds of online shops listed. Most of them are very transparent with their supply chains as well. I saved a list after looking for European sustainable clothing brands.
Sometimes they have sales too! Not often, but occasionally you can get discounts too. (Just be prepared that a T-shirt will usually cost about 40€.

Also: Learn how to take care of your clothes. How to med them, how to wash them properly, how to dry them.

I hope this is somewhat useful.

author: @raraavis7782
text:
Yes, it's the old 'a wardrobe full of clothes, but nothing to wear' problem. I mean, a large part of the clothes that are being discarded aren't even worn out or damaged, because of inferior quality. They are hardly even worn. Possibly not at all. 
They probably never fit quite right, weren't as flattering as hoped for or weren't actually suitable for the person's lifestyle (been there, done that). And if the incentive to send them back isn't very high, or they were shipped straight from China...
Doesn't help, that many people's weight tend to go up slowly but steadily at a concerningly young age already, so size changes are an issue. And for women, of course, having kids usually means their figure changes at least somewhat. 
In the sewing community, size adjustable clothes are currently *the* big theme. How to best construct clothes, that allow for going up or down at least one size, without fit issues. Whereas fast fashion is usually impossible to alter, at least if your size goes up. 
As for recommendations...Justine Leconte comes to mind. She hasn't been very active lately, but she has made quite a few in depth videos about fast fashion vs sustainable fashion and she has actual insight into the fashion industry. 
Maybe a bit tangential, but I would also recommend Tanner Leatherstein. He's a leather specialist and takes apart and critiques designer handbags. Now handbags isn't something I'm usually interested in, but it's worthwhile watching a few in regards to the whole 'recognizing quality and craftsmanship' and what something is worth debate.
I dearly wish, there was a similar channel for women's footwear. 
I also feel, taking a deep dive into body types and coloring systems is worthwhile, to be able to shop with a higher success rate. For that I would recommend AlyArt and StyleMeJen. There are loads others, of course. But those two have especially impressed me with their insights and ability to explain these concepts.

text:
I am by no means on the fast fashion side, but I'm all for a healthy discussion:

1. Fast fashion only came along recently in the last few decades.  What was Bangladesh economy like before fast fashion came along? What did these people do for a living?
2. One of the men says in the video that there's nothing else he could do other than toiling here.  So hypothetically, say by some miracle, we all stop buying fast fashion, companies start to pull out their operations, what will these people do? How will the economy reshape?
3. Before some self righteous person proudly announces that they only buy clothing Made In USA (or other developed countries), don't be naive. More often than not, garments are still made in some poor country like Bangladesh, then they reserve the last insignificant manufacturing step to be done in USA, so they can slap that Made in USA label on them. Yes i have seen that being done, first hand. 
4. In a way, are these factories actually saving some kids from prostitution/human trafficking?
5. While these poor souls barely have enough to eat and will never live a healthy long life, people in western countries are pissed when they're being called the wrong pronouns. Huh, Food for thought.

author: @pverbeek4133
text:
All of us should buy locally made goods (though materials could come from elsewhere) so all of us (meaning the whole world) can live better.

I say this after just, for the first time in a year, ordering a bunch of shirts from Amazon this week, and failed to look where they are made!
How hypocritical.  Must have been my karma to then land somehow on this clip!!!  But I simply forgot to pay attention.  
 (Luckily, I am already a low-use consumer and wear clothing until it's no good and I don't roll with 'fashion' and am averse to buying, and buying and buying like so many people do), 

I began paying attention to locally-made (for me that's the USA) about 3 years ago.  I began to buy products from Amazon that say, 'made in America' - even if they are more expensive, but knowing that environmental - and labor standards are good.  
I do this in an effort to not partake in this type of slavery which I already know is here on the other side of cheap products ordered in the USA ...
The slavery type of conditions are on the other side of the dollar, on the other side of the world.

Often you can't tell ordering on Amazon or online what the origin is.

This YouTube video has made me fully aware again and I was feeling depressed about this global situation all morning. 

The countries themselves (the ppl and their governments) where these situations are, should also not accept the conditions for their people. 

The change can only come if the effort is worldwide, every single person doing their part.

So I guess that starts with me?  And you?

Capital is always profit-driven, moving wherever labor costs are low. In the past, that was China; more recently, it has been countries in South Asia and Southeast Asia. These places have large populations but limited resources, and there aren’t many industries they can develop. Many well-known clothing companies have come to invest and build factories there. On the one hand, this does create a significant number of jobs, but on the other hand, as shown in the video, workers’ wages and health conditions are very serious issues.

Governments in poor countries are often highly corrupt, and when facing the investments brought by these big companies, they have little bargaining power. They can only cooperate with these corporations to further exploit the lowest-level workers who have no labor rights protections. Of course, this is just my own conspiracy-theory-style speculation. But when I see the market value of these large companies rising steadily, with their owners and shareholders making enormous profits, it does seem that this speculation makes at least some sense.

The people of Bangladesh are most resilient, hard working, talented and passionate people and they are good at their own craft and within different sectors. They should be honoured, celebrated for their contribution and strongly recognised. We need more strong legal policies and support systems in place to help protect businesses, employees and the national status of the country where people can be able to work within the textile industry, earn a good wage, and be able to work without having any impact on wellbeing. author: @findthemangotrees
text: I fundamentally disagree with the conclusive messaging you left with this well visualized, highly publicized, and thoughtful storytelling of this video. "We cannot delude ourselves into thinking that we can change the system these children are victims of" is a disempowering and dishonest remark to make to the 1.12 million followers you have. Sponsorship is essential for an immediate direct impact for categorically improving the lives of children to get access to the program, this is true. However, economies become extractive and enslaving such as this PRIMARILY due to the cognitive dissonance perpetuated in the populus in economies that are the buyers, as well as states that historically and presently are still enacting a practice of colonization. The predatory nature of enticing emerging and transitioning economies with the "demand" of production, is always going to destroy alternative forms of transaction, value building, and domestic trade based on innovating and fulfilling for the needs of the people in a place. Changing the system looks squarely like: divestment, reparations, designing clothes for repair and modification, providing the labor for environmental clean up, etc. Also, 'consumers not paying in to the system' is not using our collective power correctly, and it is allowing us to dissipate our necessary rage into a placated state which does not change the power structures that have been forcing these products, forcing the propaganda of their social and cultural marketing, and forcing mass populations to be their force of labour, all to generate massive waste and profits. It is not impossible get those powers out of place, why would we lie to each other, when people we care about and those we love and even ourselves are getting hurt by it? How about targeting the position holders in companies that do order placement? They will not stop without pressure. As well, it is truly important to know and get access to education about the complexity of how particular items of clothes are made. Despite automation in manufacturing & assembly for processing chips, complex machines even, the necessary operations for producing clothes is still reliant on the human labor. Ask why. What preconceived bias do we have, what limiting beliefs? Is there something standing in the way? Who is the voice of authority on the matter? Where are their interests coming from? The true cost and the real value of each item of something we wear on our bodies must be radically reimagined by people who have been living, predominantly in europe & turtle island, and essentially have been lied to their entire lives going generations back about "how things work" "why they are this way" and the biggest lie of all "that's just how it is". Changing widespread business practice to remove operations from places like Bangladesh is also only one part, areas that have been exploited in this manner for their resources (in this case human capital and environmental access), moving suddenly can be a shock to the economy, real people's lives who were once dependent on the income generated from this work (even if it was harmful to them), this still arose from a lack of access to other choices, and lack of chance for other opportunities to earn and pay money to each other to grow. It means just as much a withdrawal and an end to the harm being done by the gigantic volume of materials being produced and exported, to also think from independent businesses, organizations, governments even that have profited off of this enslavement ~ to pay back in value of the people, or for example new and smaller businesses building new relationships and new opportunities for building bridges of trade, based off of what people in Bangladesh choose to offer, if they seek or want to export goods&services at all. Decentralizing those relationships, diversifying them, and also only opening them if they are led by incentives created from within Bangladesh, not imposed from the outside. All of these are ways for people to think, to be inspired, to be motivated, and to re-examine the systems that we are a part of, participate in, and can be redesigned by our collective human ingenuity at any time. If you are someone who actually watches a video like this of your own accord because it interests you, and you finish it until the end, please trust in yourself, and in your peers, and in the millions of other people who watched it too, that yes take the immediate action available to build a relationship with someone you can help, but also do-not-ever yield your outrage or give away your desire to make a difference so easily. This is a strategy that has been used for such a long time, to maintain the status quo. Please see, that you are ALWAYS more capable than what society is going to give you permission to be. This project is so meaningful to rehumanize us in a space that is genuine with others, and to honor that with the people here I would like to offer these challenges to take forward and create from.

This is fascinating and horrific at the same time. I’ve heard about these situations, but to see it with my own eyes is very different. It’s the conditions that these amazing humans have to deal with every hour of their day that’s so heart wrenching.
It’s hard to figure out what needs to be done, because on one hand you want to free these people of this cruel life, but if we prevent places like this from existing, then what will they do? If they have no places to work, then what happens? Because I highly doubt the greedy companies would ever agree to give them decent wages or decent places and conditions to work in.
It would be different if this was on a tiny scale and you could rescue a factory of 100 people from conditions like this, but this is happening on a massive almost unfathomable scale. How does anyone correct such a large issue that’s been compounding for so many years already?

author: @sharminbrishti
text:
So many opinions on this thread. All valid questions. I'll try to shed some light on the issue. 
1. It's not only Zara and H&M. Big fashion brands that like to roast fast fashion saying only fast fashion exploits people, they also do the same. They just sell the idea "fast fashion bad" because fast fashion is hurting their business. (Levis, Calvin Klein, Adidas, Nike, Puma, Tommy Hilfiger, Gap, Giorgio Armani, Ralph Lauren and Hugo Boss, etc. make their clothes in bangladesh too.)
2. The kinds of factories this documentary showed, they don't sell to brands. They simply can't meet the standard. Brands like Zara, Calvin Klein have deals with factories that have good equipments, good working conditions, and good safety measures. That doesn't mean that the workers work less hours or are well paid. Those are also extremely exploitative, but the environment is better.
3. It's true that these fashion brands make EXTREMELY HIGH profit from selling these clothes. Everything is sold at 5 to 10 times higher prices in western markets, sometimes even higher.
4. People need these jobs. If the fashion brands pull out of Bangladesh, it's only going to cause more suffering for these people.
5. The government ain't gonna do shit. They're in on this exploitation. Human rights ain't much of a thing under dictatorships.
6. You as an western individual shouldn't feel responsible for this suffering if you're buying these clothes. But your governments are intentionally, and EXTREMELY complicit in this exploitation. They like to put on the pretense of care because they need to be liked by their people. People in general mostly have good hearts, but their worldview is shaped by heavily controlled narrative. Coming to Europe I realized how little people know about things outside the western world, and how biased their views are, it was quite shocking. The high standard of living and hyper consumption in the west is kept alive by the exploitation of these poor nations. Look up world trade organi, and the imf and world bank debt trap. 
7. I'm sorry, but you as an individual can't do much, no matter how much it breaks your heart. Western governments empower corporations to exploit poor countries. These corporations have ENORMOUS power, yes, more than a poor nation's government. But you can try to learn the root causes of such issues and hold your governments accountable for enabling corporate exploitation. They're not gonna listen to you anyway, but maybe it will give you some peace of mind knowing that you spoke up against it.

text: lived in Brazil up to my 30s, and buying clothes there, even fast fashion brands like zara, is very expensive (example: zara is considered a brand for high-middle class to rich people there. not extreme luxury but a luxury brand). So I grew accustomed to only buying clothes when I needed and on special occasions (birthday, christmas, church/family/social events). I also always shared clothes with my younger sister, my mom and one of my grandmas. Mom and grandma always had a full wardrobe, and often grandma would pull up some vintage piece out of her closet, or would keep our clothes  that were out of fashion in our eyes, just so we would pick it up again a few years later. Clothes that didnt fit anymore or were not 100% , but still usable, we would give away to other people, at least twice a year, and clothes that were too old or damaged would turn into cleaning cloths or my other grandma would cut them make clothes for our toys/barbies/dolls. Now I live in a rich country where clothing, specially these fast fashion brands are much more affordable, and yes I do get tempted sometimes to buy stuff.. but I always try to remember myself that it makes much more sense to spend more in fewer pieces of clothing that are better quality and will last longer.. and I prefer to save my money for when I do NEED to buy something, so I can spend more in a better quality thing.

author: @paolahf
text:
I think one of the best things we could do, not as an individual but as a community, is to stop making clothing and generally, superficial matters, such an important part of our identity.

I often seen young people making videos showcasing new items they acquired. A big part of their lives revolves around shopping, and therefore, their jobs. That doesn't benefit anyone. Capitalism has created a culture which prioritizes an item before an individual. You're not your thoughts or ideas (if these are not profitable), you're the brands you support and the resources you have.

Young people may try to defeat the status quo in many areas, but one fundamental one that is being neglected is building oneself as an individual beyond a brand that supports your identity. Even ideologies are turning into a form of personality now, it's not longer an interest but rather, a characteristic. Social media has only increased the depth of this issue.

author: @EmmaVB82
text:
Kinda related to a few ideas in this thread (relating to both self esteem/body image/multiple pairs of jeans! 😄) - I still have *so many* pairs of jeans in a variety of sizes from over the years, due to my size and shape changing. I lost a lot of weight 5 years ago from a combination of new medication side effects & some drawn out dental surgery dramas affecting what I could eat, so I had to buy a whole load of new clothes that actually fit (particularly things like jeans/trousers/bras/things that aren’t as flexible on sizing). Since then, the environmental conditions affecting the size and shape of my body changed in the complete other direction (hello pandemic lockdowns, and no longer walking so much on a daily basis as part of my commute!) that not only do the smaller clothes I bought no longer fit, but the ones I still had from before that time don’t either! 🤷🏻‍♀️

By this point I feel like I could open my own secondhand clothes store with things in a variety of sizes, including stacks of jeans in great condition. I’m terrible at organising myself/logistics enough to properly sell all the things mounting up around me, from clothes to electronics (thanks ADHD!), and I’m literally at the point of thinking about whether I can pay someone to do it for me, so I can be free of both the physical things taking up valuable space and the guilt from not wanting to to do damage to the environment by creating more waste, and then have the mental peace and clarity from not feeling so encumbered by all this stuff. 

(I do also donate things to various charities as well as giving away via local apps, but the financial cost of all the things I’ve accumulated over the years that I now need to replace isn’t nothing, so I definitely have a mental resistance to zeroing out that value and then having to find the money all over again. But this is probably a me problem, and the amount of mental clarity and physical space I could regain is probably worth sucking it up…) 

And even after all that, the fact is I *still* don’t have any jeans that fit me, so I still need to obtain *more* clothes! 😆😝

For a handful of years I’ve been doing my best to avoid anything with polyester and preferring natural fabrics where possible (feeling sweaty while wearing it is a more immediately noticeable problem than the environmental impact, but that’s certainly a driving factor for me too). I’m prepared to spend more money on good quality clothes that are ethically made, with sustainable materials that do less damage to the environment and make me feel more comfortable when wearing them, but I’m finding it to be a real challenge to meet all of these criteria, and also be available in plus sizes, and in long lengths. I don’t care about being “fashionable” or following trends, just finding clothes I like that fit me well and feel comfortable. 

It wouldn’t change a lot of people’s behaviour, but having knowledge of and access to suitable alternatives instead of the ever-present fast fashion stores would be really helpful. It’s a bit like the psychology behind breaking/forming habits - knowing something is “bad” is absolutely half of the battle, but unless you know and have something to replace it with, you’re much less likely to be successful.

(On that note, if anyone has recommendations for places like this to shop in the UK, or resources containing other lists/recs, I’m all ears!)
